title: At the peak of hiking season, Colorado sees 5,350 lightning strikes on any day in July. Here's how to stay safe.
author: Ryan Spencer
description: As summer peaks in the Colorado Rocky Mountains, summer is not only a bustling season for hiking, summiting the state's famous 14ers and enjoying the great outdoors. It's also the busiest time of year…
content:
Lightning strikes over Dillon Reservoir Monday, July 31, 2023.
Curtis DeVore/Courtesy photo
As summer peaks in the Colorado Rocky Mountains, summer is not only a bustling season for hiking, summiting the state's famous 14ers and enjoying the great outdoors. It's also the busiest time of year for lightning strikes.
Lightning is one of the most powerful forces in nature, and while it is beautiful to watch it is also extremely dangerous , according to the National Parks Service. The National Weather Service reports that on any given day in July, there are 5,350 lightning flashes in Colorado.
'No place outside is safe from lightning,' the Colorado Search and Rescue Association wrote in a recent social media post. 'So watch the forecast when you're planning a backcountry outing and stay alert for signs of an impending thunderstorm, regardless of the forecast, while you're out.'
Last year, 14 people in the U.S. died from lightning strikes, according to the National Weather Service. While nobody was killed by lightning in Colorado in 2023, an early morning lightning strike frightened two hikers climbing Quandary Peak, a 14,000-foot peak, ahead of the Fourth of July last year.
Earlier this year, a lightning strike killed a cattle rancher in Jackson County, marking the first lightning fatality in the state since 2020.
Still, the National Lightning Safety Council reports that Colorado has among the most lightning deaths in the country, ranking third in the nation for fatalities between 2006 and 2023, with 24 fatalities in that time. For a state known for its outdoor recreation industry, that isn't too surprising since outdoor leisure activities are among the most common activities people are engaged in when they are hurt or killed by lightning.
Between 2006 and 2023, fishing was the activity that contributed to the most U.S. lightning fatalities, with 41 deaths, or just less than 10% of all lightning deaths, according to the National Weather Service. Farming or ranching, camping and boating each accounted for about 25 lightning deaths in that timespan. This graph from the National Weather Service shows what outdoor activities have the greatest risk of lightning strikes. National Weather Service/Courtesy image
When recreating, no place outdoors is safe from lightning, but making the right decisions can reduce the risk of being harmed by a lightning strike. Since lightning can strike outward as far as 10 miles from a thunderstorm, being within earshot of thunder is a good indication that the storm is within striking distance.
Mountain summits, high-Alpine terrain and wide open areas, including water bodies, are among the most dangerous areas and should be avoided if there are any signs of thunderstorms, according to the National Weather Service. Being near tall objects, such as trees that are taller relative to other surrounding trees, is also especially dangerous.
No one should ever take cover from a thunderstorm in a cave or beneath an overhang or cliff, as lightning can travel through the rock, according to the National Parks Service. Objects like tall trees, fences, power lines, windmills or poles that could conduct electricity should also be avoided.
Before a storm hits, people recreating in the backcountry should leave high-risk areas including mountainsides, descending through gullies rather than on ridgelines, if possible. When outdoors, getting below treeline is among the safer options for those climbing in the mountains, while low-lying depressions in the ground can also provide more safety than open areas.
But nothing is as safe as getting back inside a modern building or inside a metal-topped vehicle. The National Weather Service has a motto for that: 'When thunder roars, go indoors!' A lightning storm in summer 2023 yielded this amazing bolt of lightning on the side of Buffalo Mountain as seen from Silverthorne. Ruth Carroll/Courtesy photo

title: Moffat County Balloon Festival to soar with expansive schedule
author: Andy Bockelman
description: One of Craig's favorite summertime happenings is just around the corner with a weekend swollen as big as a balloon in terms of activities. The Moffat County Ballon Festival is entering its 14th year…
content:
Moffat County Balloon Festival takes place Aug. 2 to 4 at Loudy-Simpson Park, featuring hot-air balloon launches, live music and multiple activities throughout the day.
Billy Schuerman / For the Craig Press
One of Craig's favorite summertime happenings is just around the corner with a weekend swollen as big as a balloon in terms of activities.
The Moffat County Ballon Festival is entering its 14th year with a full itinerary of entertainment from Friday-Sunday at Loudy-Simpson Park. The event will feature hot air balloon launches early each morning, weather-permitting, with organizers expecting a dozen pilots or more.
Apart from a Friday night concert at downtown Craig's Alice Pleasant Park, all other activities will happen around Loudy-Simpson Park, with most taking place Saturday.
Among the returning features are the Memorial Regional Health Flying Colors 5K in the morning and a variety of classic vehicles from across the years at the Colorado Cruisers Car Show throughout the day Saturday.
Attendees can walk away with big money or prizes in numerous outlets, including afternoon bingo or the Northwest Colorado Health Rubber Ducky Race along the Yampa River.
The Cardboard Boat Regatta on the Loudy ponds will offer a purse of $2,000 in prizes for the fastest paddlers, best boat designs and most epic fails. Cuatro Estados, an RV group from the Four Corners states, competes in the Cardboard Boat Regatta on Saturday, Aug. 5, 2023, in Craig. While they weren't the fastest, the group won second place for best design. Eli Pace/Craig Press
This year will also see more children's activities, said organizer Randy Looper.
In addition to bounce houses, slides, face painting and other activities, new features this year will include a kite-making and flying session and a Dino Dig hosted by the Colorado Northwestern Community College paleontology department.
'We don't want too much wind in the morning for the balloons, but hopefully we get some in the afternoon so kids can fly kites on the soccer fields with their parents,' Looper said. 'The Dino Dig will be in the volleyball pit for kids to dig in the sand and put together their own dinosaur bones.'
An Olympic-themed competition among balloon pilots will also provide a new type of entertainment.
Early afternoon music will be provided by The Lost Junction Band and Tucker Rose before the evening sounds of '60s and '70s tribute band Stuck on Vinyl, followed by Project Foreigner a cover band paying homage to the creator of 'Hot Blooded,' 'Cold As Ice,' and many more hits, which will take place during the evening balloon glow. Pilots light up their hot air balloons during the ballon glow at the Moffat County Hot Air Balloon Festival on Saturday, Aug. 6, 2022, at Loudy-Simpson Park in Craig. Eli Pace/Craig Press
Looper added that Foreigner's recent induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame made them an ideal choice.
'I've seen them three times on the Front Range, and they're just amazing,' Looper said of the headliner.
He added that while there is registration required for some events, the festival as a whole has no admission costs.
'It's a full day, it's free and just great for every age,' Looper said.
For full details, visit MCBalloonFestival.com . Iver Ringle, front, and his mom, Cassandra, take off at the start of their race during the Cardboard Boat Regatta at the Moffat County Hot Air Balloon Festival on Saturday, Aug. 5, 2023, in Craig. The duo won the Titanic Award for the best sinking. Eli Pace/Craig Press

title: Health column: In case of an emergency, Memorial Regional Health promotes resources to keep residents' information current, ready
author: Memorial Regional Health
description: In an emergency, having up-to-date medical information is crucial for timely and accurate care. Memorial Regional Health has teamed up with community and emergency services in Moffat County to offer…
content:
Memorial Regional Health partners with community and emergency services in Moffat County to provide lifesaving programs, including Yellow Dot and Vial of L.I.F.E.
Memorial Regional Health/Courtesy photo
In an emergency, having up-to-date medical information is crucial for timely and accurate care.
Memorial Regional Health has teamed up with community and emergency services in Moffat County to offer programs like Vial of L.I.F.E. and Yellow Dot.
These initiatives ensure that community member's critical health information is always current and accessible, streamlining emergency responses and enhancing personalized care.
The Yellow Dot program is a community initiative designed to assist first responders in the event of an emergency.
A medical form is placed in the participant's car and is designed to supply first responders with critical information about that person during an emergency, when they might not be able to communicate themselves. Participation is voluntarily and authorizes the disclosure to and use of medical information by first responders for the purpose of offering assistance when involved in an accident.
The Vial of L.I.F.E. (Lifesaving Information for Emergencies) kit helps individuals keep their complete medical information and have it readily accessible at home for emergency personnel. Each kit consists of two decals and a Medical Information form with instructions: Fill out form: Answer questions about your health and medications on the medical information form. Place on refrigerator: Securely tape the form to the front of your refrigerator. (Recommended to store inside plastic baggie.) Stick on the decals: Place one decal on your refrigerator and one decal on your front door at eye level.
This ensures that crucial medical details are available when a patient cannot communicate or remember them. The Vial of L.I.F.E. program is especially useful for senior citizens and is supported by the senior centers, fire departments and other community organizations in the community.
Fill out all program forms at your next appointment at MRH or contact Megan O'Toole for more information at megan.otoole@memorialrh.org or call 970-761-0003.
MRH is dedicated to fostering a healthier community through proactive and comprehensive approaches. By providing community resources, educational outreach, support groups, and partnerships with local organizations, MRH ensures that residents receive the care and support they need especially during emergencies.
These efforts prioritize accessible health care, addressing immediate medical concerns while also empowering individuals with the knowledge and resources necessary for long-term health, well-being and peace of mind.

title: Guest column: Western Colorado leaders plan for an ‘all of the above' energy future
author: Greg Brophy
description: Producing energy for the nation is part of Western Colorado's DNA. It is every bit as important as farming, ranching and the outdoor economy to the region's identity. Extreme voices in the climate…
content:
Producing energy for the nation is part of Western Colorado's DNA. It is every bit as important as farming, ranching and the outdoor economy to the region's identity.
Extreme voices in the climate debate have argued that Western Colorado should abandon energy production as part of its identity. They want to ban oil and natural gas production on federal lands and celebrate the retirement of coal-fired power plants in communities like Hayden.
But those voices are wrong. They are blind to the fact that oil and natural gas will continue to be needed in the world for decades, even under aggressive targets for cutting carbon emissions to net-zero by 2050. And they ignore the reality that the infrastructure and workforce that supported the production of coal-fired electricity can be used to produce other kinds of energy too.
With the right leadership, a Western Colorado energy sector that once depended mostly on the production of three fuels — oil, gas and coal — can expand into an 'all of the above' energy sector that produces many fuels.
Planning for that future was the focus of the second annual Energy Summit, held late last month in Montrose. The conference was convened by a nonprofit called Joint Organizations Leading Transition, and supported by dozens of public and private entities including county governments, utilities, rural electric cooperatives and the regional advocacy group Club 20.
The event focused on the wide range of fuels and energy technologies that are well-suited to Western Colorado and their potential for bringing investment and jobs to the region.
Advanced geothermal energy, for example, can leverage the workforce and the technologies of the oil and natural gas industry to create a new source of baseload electricity. Just like oil and gas companies drill thousands of feet below the surface seeking energy deposits, geothermal developers drill deep below the surface to find heat.
Energy storage is another promising option. The version of this technology that gets most attention, of course, is the large-scale battery. But in Colorado, we can leverage our decades of experience with hydroelectricity to pursue another way to store electricity from wind farms and solar panels for use when the wind isn't blowing and the sun isn't shining.
Pumped-hydro storage uses electricity from renewables to move water uphill to a reservoir. Then, when the power grid needs more electricity, the stored water is released and powers a turbine when it runs back downhill. Currently, there are at least two pumped storage locations being explored in Colorado right now, including one in the Yampa River Valley between Hayden and Craig.
Western Colorado's abundant natural gas reserves can also help deliver both energy security and emissions reductions, both here in the United States and internationally. Natural gas is the cleanest hydrocarbon fuel, with around 50% of the carbon emissions of coal. It can also be used as a feedstock for hydrogen and ammonia, and with the addition of carbon capture technology, natural gas can have an even lower carbon footprint than it does today.
The next generation of nuclear plants could also find a home in Western Colorado. Construction has already started on a new reactor in southwest Wyoming where an existing coal-fired power plant is due for retirement, and there's every reason to think that same concept could work in Northwest Colorado.
The selection of a retiring coal-plant site is not coincidental. The new nuclear plant, roughly one-third the size of a typical reactor, will use the existing power lines and other infrastructure that supported the coal plant's operation, making the project less expensive to complete.
The same concept of using existing infrastructure to attract new energy sources also applies for renewable energy. Planning officials in Routt County have been approached by renewable energy developers who specialize in solar and energy storage about building new facilities near the transmission lines that serve the coal-fired power plant in Hayden.
Along the same lines, Xcel Energy is exploring a biomass power plant, fueled with beetle-killed trees and other forest waste, and energy storage facilities that would connect to the grid where the coal plant currently operates.
This is just a brief snapshot of the discussions that took place during last month's conference in Montrose about the future of energy in Western Colorado. The event was an excellent example of the region's continued leadership on energy issues, now and decades into the future.
After all, as the saying goes, there is no better way to predict the future than to create it yourself.

title: Colorado Parks and Wildlife confirms eight sheep killed by wolves
author: Meg Soyars Van Hauen
description: Colorado Parks and Wildlife confirmed that eight sheep in Grand County were killed by wolves. The agency updated its Gray Wolf Depredation Report webpage on Wednesday. According to the webpage, the…
content:
On the property where the sheep were killed, a wolf is captured on a game camera carrying off an animal's leg. The animal is believed to be a calf and the image was captured shortly before the sheep were found dead.
Courtesy photo
Colorado Parks and Wildlife confirmed that eight sheep in Grand County were killed by wolves. The agency updated its Gray Wol f Depredation Report webpage on Wednesday. According to the webpage, the depredations occurred on Sunday, and the investigation is still in progress. This is the 14th wolf depredation incident confirmed in Colorado since reintroduction.
On Sunday, Colorado Parks and Wildlife officials responded to another possible wolf depredation in Grand County. Two sheep were involved — a lamb and a ewe.
'The field investigation, which included a necropsy, found injuries consistent with wolf depredation,' stated Parks and Wildlife in an email. '… This is still an ongoing investigation.'
According to the agency, the depredations occurred sometime in the late evening on Saturday, and early morning Sunday. Once the depredation of the two sheep is confirmed, the agency will update the Gray Wolf Depredation Report webpage. Parks and Wildlife officials also received a report of missing sheep in the area.
On July 17, officials confirmed the first wolf depredation of a single sheep in Grand County. This was the first sheep that had been killed or injured by a wolf in the county since reintroduction .
Parks and Wildlife has confirmed 13 wolf depredation incidents in Colorado since they were released in December 2023.

title: Country music, demolition derby, rodeo happenings all part of Moffat County Fair fun
author: Andy Bockelman
description: If it's early August, that can only mean one thing at the Moffat County Fairgrounds. Lots of action. A wide variety of entertainment is on the docket for the Moffat County Fair this week, with...
content:
Country singer Eli Mosley will be the headliner for the Moffat County Fair Friday, Aug. 9, 2024. Events throughout the week include a rodeo, a demolition derby and more.
Courtesy Photo
If it's early August, that can only mean one thing at the Moffat County Fairgrounds. Lots of action.
A wide variety of entertainment is on the docket for the Moffat County Fair this week, with a combination of good old-fashioned down and dirty activities as well as lofty entertainment.
The musical headliner for this year's fair is country act Eli Mosley, taking the stage Friday evening in the fairgrounds arena.
While this is his first time performing in Craig, Mosley has family ties to the area. His grandmother, Etta Mae Mosley, was a Denver native — and daughter of the owner of P. Hicks Cadle All American Seasoning business — who served as a teacher in Craig in the 1940s. She was married to his grandfather, William Mosley, just days before he shipped out to serve in World War II flying missions between India and China, a route known as 'the Hump' for its path over the Himalayas.
As one who served in the Marine Corps himself — one of many in his family with military distinctions — that element of duty plays heavily into Mosley's music, as well as the effect that service can have on family members.
'I've got a song called 'Soldier's Wife,' and I'll meet veterans' wives who are really touched by that,' he said. 'Songs about divorce or a baby on the way or marriage, whatever it may be, that's why you do it. Family stories.'
He noted that he's had audience members who have told him that his music saved their life, and such stories embolden him as a songwriter.
'My heart and soul is always in the live shows, because that's where you get to meet the people that your music is reaching. Without being able to meet everybody like that, it's hard to have motivation to keep making music,' he said. 'I'm not in it for the money or the fame or popularity or any of that nonsense. It has everything to do with people out there on the road.'
Playing all types of venues as a Nashville artist, rural settings tend to be his favorite, and he's performed at Nebraska State Fair, Wisconsin Country Thunder, Cody Wyoming Nite Rodeo, South Dakota Buffalo Roundup, Arizona Country Thunder and Cheyenne Frontier Days, to name a few.
Having released three albums in the past decade, Mosley is in the process of putting the finishing touches on a fourth for release later this year. He also runs a Florida cattle operation, which he said keeps him in line with his family legacy in agriculture.
'I've been all over the place, but places like Nebraska, Wyoming and Colorado suit my lifestyle really well,' Mosley said.
He added that his sound touches on multiple country styles but is primarily honky-tonk in nature and aimed at keeping all ages engaged.
'It's gonna be a good, high-energy, family-friendly country music show,' he said.
The performance by Mosley will cap off a busy night that includes area band Tucker Rose as an opening act.
Before the music gets started, spectators will first hear a wholly different type of sound with the Demolition Derby. The display of utter auto annihilation will include multiple classes of cars and trucks competing for dominance with a sizable purse at stake for those who prove the toughest.
The derby and concerts are a package deal, with everything kicking off at 6 p.m. Friday. Kids in the 11 to 14 age division collect their animals for the 2023 Catch-a-Pig Contest during the Moffat County Fair. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
The Friday action of revving engines and guitar twang will be preceded by Thursday's cowboy-centric happenings, a lineup that includes the PRCA/WPRA rodeo events for the more experienced riders as well as the Rocky Mountain Mini Broncs and Mini Bulls for younger athletes and the return of the Catch-a-Pig Contest for kids of all experience levels.
Tickets for both Thursday and Friday events are $20 in advance, $30 at the gate and free to kids 7 and younger. Registration for Catch-a-Pig will be available at the gate.
Following a week full of showing and selling animals and presenting 4-H projects, Saturday will be the big finale for the Moffat County Fair with a day focusing on fun. The Bucket Calf Contest, Cutest Baby Contest and Sheep Lead Contest will be part of Saturday activities at Moffat County Fair. Andy Bockelman/staff
The Cowboy Baby Contest, Sheep Lead Contest and Bucket Calf Contest give future farmers and ranchers their due, while Derby Days activities for dog and horse let the animals take to the track and compete.
Activities throughout the day include the pancake breakfast, pie-eating contest and wine and beer brewing contest, among others.
For more information on schedules and registration, visit MoffatCountyfair.com .

title: Health column: Tips to keep your student healthy as the school year begins
author: UCHealth
description: Students will soon return to school with new backpacks, high hopes and possibly some butterflies in their tummy. Unfortunately, they can return home with germs and viruses that lead to respiratory…
content:
Students will soon return to school with new backpacks, high hopes and possibly some butterflies in their tummy. Unfortunately, they can return home with germs and viruses that lead to respiratory illness and stomach flu that could sideline them, their siblings and parents.
'Back to school means close exposure of children with each other in the classroom, at sporting events and at other extracurricular activities,' said Brooke Packard, a physician assistant with UCHealth Yampa Valley Medical Center. 'Those things make it that much easier for germs to be spread, which can lead to kids brining viruses home to their families.'
But, transitioning from outside fun to indoor classes doesn't have to mean that coughs, colds and flus are part of the new school year.
'Something as easy and simple as washing your hands can't be underestimated for maintaining good health,' said Packard. 'It's at the top of the list in terms of good basic hygiene.'
No matter the age, everyone should practice good handwashing techniques that include scrubbing between fingers and for an extended time, say long enough to sing the first verse of 'Happy Birthday.' It's especially important to wash hands after using the bathroom and blowing your nose, which can be two main sources of germ spreading.
While it might be tempting to send children to school when they're not feeling well due to busy parent schedules, Packard advises against it. Not only will your child not have a good day at school due to being under the weather, they will likely be passing along viruses to their classmates and teachers.
'Keep them home and wait until they're feeling better before letting them return to class,' said Packard.
If and when your child brings home unwanted bugs, wiping off high-touch service areas in the kitchen and bathroom with a bleach-based cleanser is recommended, along with swapping out towels, changing sheets and ventilating a home with fresh air. It's a good idea to have fever reducers and a humidifier on hand to help relieve symptoms, and the ever-reliable BRAT diet, comprised of bananas, rice, applesauce and toast, is still reliable if the stomach flu hits.
An immune system that is heartened with a balanced diet makes it that much easier to fight off infections, said Packard, and that includes eating a healthy breakfast and packing a lunch with fruits and vegetables, protein and carbohydrates.
'Try to eat the rainbow every day — fruits and veggies of all sorts of colors – as maintaining a healthy diet is key to maintaining a healthy immune system,' she said.
Proper hydration, between three and eight cups of water per day depending upon a child's age and physical activity level, is also key. She suggests a thermos or fun water bottle to encourage children, especially younger ones, to drink water. Packard is a big believer in vitamin D for people of all ages, especially in the winter when more time is spent inside.
'If there's one vitamin that everyone can take all of their lives, it's D,' she said.
No matter what the age, sleep is essential to good health and especially important for growing children and teenagers, Packard said. Most kids need an average of 10 hours of sleep a night, which can at times be a difficult ask, especially for high school students busy with academic, athletic and extracurricular commitments. She suggests:
• Developing a bedtime routine whenever possible.
• Limiting screen time after dinner, and shutting off phones and computers two hours before sleep.
• Taking a bath or shower or reading before lights out.
'It's amazing what lack of sleep can do to your health,' said Packard. 'Sleep is so important and so much of it is dependent on getting into a deeper sleep pattern.'
A healthy mind is just as important as a healthy body, and both need to co-exist in harmony, Packard said. She suggests lots of fresh air, exercise and fun with family and friends. Time spent together also presents moments for parents to check in with children about any stressors or anxiety, and look for possible signs of depression or mental health struggles.
'Carve out family time — take a walk, go to the park, eat dinner together,' said Packard. 'Ask questions and stay connected with your kids.'

title: Wildfire flares up in Moffat County west of Craig
author: Staff Report
description: A wildfire is burning along U.S. Highway 40 in Moffat County west of Craig. The fire appears to be about three or four miles away from the Western Knolls subdivision, and there are a handful...
content:
Smoke rises from a wildfire burning west of Craig in Moffat County on Wednesday, Aug. 7, 2024.
Bonnie Stewart/Craig Press
A wildfire is burning along U.S. Highway 40 in Moffat County west of Craig.
The fire appears to be about three or four miles away from the Western Knolls subdivision, and there are a handful of homes in the area.
According to the Moffat County Sheriff's Office, the blaze near Moffat County Roads 90 and 174, and it was not threatening any structures on Wednesday.
The fire was reported after 3 p.m. Wednesday. According to Watch Duty, a nonprofit wildfire reporting app, the blaze has grown to 150 acres, and the Moffat County Sheriff's Office along with the Bureau of Land Management and Craig Fire are working to contain the fire.
However, at 4:30 p.m., the sheriff's office reported the fire had only burned about 10 acres.
Watch Duty has dubbed the blaze 'the Big Gulch Fire.'
According to the Moffat County Sheriff's Office, the Browns Park National Wildlife Refuge, which is northwest of the fire, is currently under Stage 2 fire restrictions with the extremely dry vegetation conditions in Northwestern Colorado.
This developing story will be updated when more information becomes available. Watch Duty shows a fire burning west of Craig in Moffat County. According to Watch Duty, the fire had grown to about 150 acres by Wednesday evening, Aug. 7, 2024. Courtesy photo

title: Northwest Colorado health care initiative Choose When goes statewide
author: Staff Report
description: A nonprofit health care initiative called Choose When that was started by philanthropic women in Routt County in spring 2017 has now expanded across the state. The Choose When program offers long…
content:
briefs
A nonprofit health care initiative called Choose When that was started by philanthropic women in Routt County in spring 2017 has now expanded across the state.
The Choose When program offers long-acting reversible contraception for income-challenged women. It was transferred to the nonprofit Caring for Colorado Foundation in October 2023 to grow the offering into a statewide program. Caring for Colorado adopted the Choose When regional model of individual and foundation fundraising to offset the costs of contraception — including long-acting methods that can cost up to $1,000 — for people with financial barriers.
The foundation recently awarded the first round of $600,000 in Choose When funding that includes more funding for Northwest Colorado and 23 other grants that will help safety-net clinics reach 38 counties throughout the state, according to Amy Maillet, strategic communications director at Caring for Colorado.
The funding continues to be available for women in Routt, Moffat, Jackson, Grand and Rio Blanco counties through Northwest Colorado Health.
'For women's health, the right to choose when to become pregnant promotes better health outcomes and improved self-sufficiency rates,' said Stephanie Einfeld, CEO at Northwest Colorado Health.

title: Colorado think tank says mountain lion hunting ban would cost millions as supporters call foul
author: Elliott Wenzler
description: Supporters and opponents of a ballot measure that would ban bobcat and mountain lion hunting in Colorado are arguing over the financial impacts of the proposal after a conservative-leaning think tank…
content:
The Common Sense Institute projected the change in hunting regulations — if approved by voters in November — would cost Colorado Parks and Wildlife millions of dollars annually.
Courtesy photo
Supporters and opponents of a ballot measure that would ban bobcat and mountain lion hunting in Colorado are arguing over the financial impacts of the proposal after a conservative-leaning think tank released a study on the topic this week.
The Common Sense Institute projected the change in hunting regulations — if approved by voters in November — would cost Colorado Parks and Wildlife millions of dollars annually. But the group proposing the measure, Cats Aren't Trophies, is calling foul on that math.
'It's really just pseudoscience,' said Samantha Miller, the campaign manager for the group.
The Common Sense Institute report claims, based on 2023 data, the state would lose around $410,000 and $15,000 annually in mountain lion and bobcat hunting license sales, respectively. Those combined represent less than 0.4% of the revenue for the agency's wildlife operations.
The analysis goes on to foresee a significantly greater loss in revenue if the mountain lion population increases due to the lack of hunting, ultimately diminishing game populations like elk and mule deer.
'The dynamic impact ranges from $3.6 million to $5.8 million — 9 to 14 times larger — when accounting for lost elk and mule deer permit revenue affected by an increase in mountain lion population,' according to the Common Sense Institute study, which references predicted annual impacts.
The authors came to that figure by assuming the mountain lions that wouldn't be hunted would kill at least one elk or deer per week, resulting in a loss of hunting license sales for those animals.
While the impact on decreasing mountain lion and bobcat hunting licenses is accurate, the second calculation is flawed, said Erik Molvar, a wildlife biologist with the Western Watersheds Project and an advocate for Initiative 91.
'You cannot assume that because you will have more mountain lions on the landscape, that you will have fewer mule deer and fewer elk,' Molvar said.
DJ Summers, an author on the Common Sense Institute report, said it was the organization's assumption that those elk and deer kills would impact the overall species' populations.
Colorado Parks and Wildlife is prohibited from taking a position for or against the initiative and declined to comment on the study that looked at budget impacts, said Travis Duncan, a spokesperson for the agency.
Colorado Parks and Wildlife is an enterprise agency, meaning it's almost entirely funded by fees, such as those from hunting tags, rather than taxes.
In 2023, there were nearly 30,000 elk hunted and about 500 mountain lions. Mountain lion hunting season, which has an annual cap set by Colorado Parks and Wildlife, is between November and March.
The initiative was approved for the November ballot earlier this month after proponents turned in enough signatures from registered voters to require a vote on the topic.
Initiative 91 reads, in part: 'The voters of Colorado find and declare that any trophy hunting of mountain lions, bobcats, or lynx is inhumane, serves no socially acceptable or ecologically beneficial purpose and fails to further public safety.'
If approved by a majority of voters, those who violate the measure would be guilty of a Class 1 misdemeanor, punishable by up to a year in jail, a fine of up to $1,000 or both. They could also be subject to a five-year suspension of their wildlife license.
The initiative makes exceptions for killing the wild cats to defend a person, livestock or pets. It also makes exceptions for depredating animals and accidents, such as vehicle and animal collisions.
Opponents of the measure and initiative have argued that biologists and wildlife experts at Colorado Parks and Wildlife should be left to manage the populations and hunting permits.
The Common Sense Institute study was one of several the think tank plans to produce on Colorado ballot issues.
'We did this because we wanted to follow the wolf introduction that happened last ballot,' said Summers, one of the study's authors. 'We knew simply that this would be something that gets a lot of people's attention.'
Other items that have been approved for the ballot relate to property taxes and abortion access.
Elliott Wenzler is the Western Slope politics reporter for the Craig Press and its sister publications in Glenwood Springs, Vail, Steamboat Springs, Craig, Summit County and Grand County. Reach her at ewenzler@swiftcom.com.

title: Pipi's Pasture: Hot summer days
author: Diane Prather
description: Every winter it's so cold that we can't wait for summer. Then every summer we experience a real hot spell, and we can't wait for winter. There doesn't seem to be much time that is...
content:
Every winter it's so cold that we can't wait for summer. Then every summer we experience a real hot spell, and we can't wait for winter.
There doesn't seem to be much time that is 'just right' when it comes to the temperature, and it doesn't seem that we're ever satisfied either. So now that we're in the midst of hot summer days, just what can be said about them?
• There's a cat in the shade under every tree here at Pipi's Pasture, and there are a lot of trees and a lot of cats.
• Likewise, on summer pasture the cattle and sheep are hunting up shade under wherever trees can be found.
• Hot temperatures, low humidity and other factors are contributing to wildfire threats, and we're so grateful to the firefighters who work so hard to protect property, humans and animals.
• This year's infestation of flies and other insects has left me with a healthy respect for animals that have to put up with them; I'm glad we put fly tags in our cows' ears — I wish I had one.
• If you didn't have a skillet, you could probably fry an egg on the sidewalk — maybe even a hamburger.
• When walking next to a body of water, such as a pool, lake, cow watering hole or even a sprinkler, one has the urge to jump in.
• It's not winter, but we still need gloves to maneuver the hot steering wheel after it has been in the sun for awhile.
• Wet clothes, hung out on hot days, dry in a hurry.
• These hot days have me out early so that I can water the lawn and finish other chores before it's way too hot.
• My one tomato garden enjoys the sun as long as it is watered, and it is producing some tomatoes.
• Grocery shopping is done early in the morning when it's cool enough to load those big bags of purchases into the car and then out again when at home.
• It's hard to get into housecleaning when it's so hot.
• There's always something, plant or animal, around Pipi's Pasture to need water, including the deer who jump into the yard at night to eat the leaves off the elm trees and the robins who hop around the sprinkler on the lawn.
• A fan is a necessity at night, but did you ever notice how it cools off by morning?
• What a wonderful treat to find the sky to the west darkened with storm clouds when I walked outdoors early this morning and to hear a few drops of rain on the stovepipe a little later; I don't think it was forecast but wonderfully appreciated.
And so we're into the hot days of summer, but never fear for all too soon we'll be into the cold days of winter.

Colorado Parks and Wildlife recently announced a new website design.
CPW
Colorado Parks and Wildlife launched a website redesign Wednesday in hopes of revamping the agency's information flows and offering a more visually appealing site.
'Reimagining a website as robust as ours is no easy task, and while we know changes are always a challenge, we think you'll find this website more dynamic, functional, and easier for you, our customers and partners, to use,' said CPW Branding and Communications Section Manager Rebecca Ferrell, in a news release.
The agency says it has reviewed all web content at CPW.state.co.us to eliminate repetitions and consolidate pages while updating necessary information. The new site will provide translations into multiple languages and eventually a chatbot for inquiries.
Previously saved bookmarks may not be redirected and users may have a harder time finding information as quickly on an internet search in the short term. The website redesign was funded through a grant from Great Outdoors Colorado.

title: Lance Scranton: It's an epidemic
author: Lance Scranton
description: The school year has started and the grind begins in earnest as teachers settle into the everyday realities of spending hours a day with young people. It's no secret that there are a number of...
content:
The school year has started and the grind begins in earnest as teachers settle into the everyday realities of spending hours a day with young people. It's no secret that there are a number of concerns being shared by the experts as public education takes its lumps and most of our once-trusted institutions take it on the chin. It's not that we shouldn't cast a critical eye on the organizations that we count on to preserve the cultural values that make this a functioning republic that is capable of figuring out how to figure out the direction we need to go so we can all live that American Dream.
Fortunately, we are in an election year so most of our ire is directed toward candidates for office of various stripes and colors. But the challenge remains the same and those of us who retain a sense of patriotic duty and continue a hopeful view into the future that provides the same opportunities for our children that this country has afforded for many of us. However, the number of people who are getting the most attention seem to be the ones who hope that our best days are behind us.
The epidemic is apparent all over the news, social media and even in our local culture. Excitement abounds in the direction of a downward trajectory as social worries, regional wars and political wrangling have taken center stage. It seems like things are just way too out of control to be anything but disastrous. So what do you do, where do you look, how can you move forward with any kind of confidence?
The thing about an epidemic is that it will run its course and come November we will elect a new leader for our country and there will be optimism from at least half the country. We will likely have one of the most closely watched and hotly contested elections in recorded history. Something will likely take place that throws the results into question, no matter who is declared the winner.
But, we will get through the toughest part by doing what Americans do best — get busy trying to figure out how to make things right. We will all do what we think is best to get on with the rest of our lives and hopefully be more determined to make the future look as good as it can for the ones we care most about.
According to the plan our local power plant will begin to shut down as will our coal mines and the once improbable will become our new reality. But the thing about plans is that they are often forced into an adjustment and no matter how much we think we know about what will happen in the future; we will never be 100% correct. People are definitely going to be affected, businesses will be forced to make changes, and our town will face the future without something that has given us economic security for so many years.
So we'll just have to figure it out and move on into a place that we've never been before. We can continue an epidemic of worry and negativity or take a shot of reality and realize that the challenges we have over the next four years will make or break how we determine what our future will look like. We can't control the things we have no control over but we do have a responsibility to do our part to keep moving forward and make the very best out of what will be our future!
Lance Scranton is a career educator and has made his home in Moffat County for the past 25 years. He offers his views and opinions as part of the ongoing conversation about our community, country and world. Reach him at lance.scranton@consultant.com .

title: Community Connections: Mentors in schools make a difference
author: Lindsay Kohler
description: Take a moment with me, and think back to when you were a middle school student (some of us will have to think back further than others). Remember what it felt like to try to...
content:
Partners for Youth's School-Based Mentors program helps students in Routt and Moffat counties by providing high quality one-on-one mentoring.
Partners for Youth/Courtesy photo
Take a moment with me, and think back to when you were a middle school student (some of us will have to think back further than others). Remember what it felt like to try to navigate social dynamics, multiple teachers, homework, family and the list goes on.
Now imagine that as a middle school student, you've had some hard things happen in your life. You're new to school, quiet, shy and you generally avoid interacting with others. Every day you sit alone at lunch and look at your lap while you eat. Your teachers and school counselors notice this, and offer to connect you with a mentor in school.
You agree, as do your parents, so you start spending about an hour with your mentor once each week. Sometimes, your time together is spent catching up school work. Sometimes it's talking about how things are going for you at home, and sometimes you're just enjoying casual conversation. In general, you like this time because it is just you and your mentor, and the mentor is not a therapist, teacher, coach or principal. Your mentor is someone you can talk to, trust and feel safe with.
Thanks to your time with your mentor and consistent support from teachers and other school staff, you start socializing with peers in and out of school, participating in class and turning in your school work on time. At one point, you're having a really hard day, and your feelings build up so much that you let them all out to your mentor, and storm out of the room.
For the next couple of weeks, your mentor checks in with you, but doesn't pressure you to meet, and eventually you stop by their office and update them on everything you've had going on recently. You're able to apologize to your mentor and thank them for checking in with you over the last few weeks, all because you've developed a safe and trusting relationship with them.
By the end of the school year, you still have your hard days, but you're going to school regularly, you've made friends and you've connected with the adults at your school.
Come back to the present moment and consider how impactful it was for this student to have an additional trusted adult to go to at school. This is what Partners for Youth provides through our School-Based Mentoring services.
Our School-Based Mentors work 20-25 hours each week in Routt County and Moffat County schools to provide high quality one-on-one mentoring to vulnerable youth. The Partners program hires, screens and trains School-Based Mentors, and we collaborate with school counselors and social workers, teachers, and administrators to implement the program.
The story above is just one example among many of how an additional trusted adult in school can be a resource, advocate, supporter and connector for student. We are thrilled to enter our second year of providing a School-Based Mentor at Craig Middle School, and to continue our collaboration with multiple schools in Routt County.
For more information about Partners for Youth and School-Based Mentoring, visit PartnersYouth.org .

title: Letter: A community can end overdose deaths
description: When someone deeply cares about a cause, society calls them passionate. Well, I am not passionate; I am angry. I am angry that every five minutes someone dies of a preventable drug overdose. I am...
content:
When someone deeply cares about a cause, society calls them passionate. Well, I am not passionate; I am angry. I am angry that every five minutes someone dies of a preventable drug overdose. I am angry that despite the many ways America has adapted over the decades, there is still a war on drugs, and my community members are casualties. Mostly, I am terrified.
I am terrified that I will one day lose a loved one to an illicit fentanyl overdose. Problematic drug use has been met with the same archaic approach for decades: We jail the user, shame the user and turn our backs on the user. The problem is this approach has failed.
According to the Centers for Disease Control, since 1999 almost one million people have died from an overdose, and 500,000 of those were related to opioids. Drug use is not going away, and drugs become more dangerous every day with additives like Xylazine. What can be done? Harm reduction is an evidence-based approach to drug use that prioritizes mitigating risks associated with drug use for the user and the community. You can do your part and take a stand.
Find out how your community is responding to drug use and ask them to adopt a harm reduction framework policy, help break negative stigmas associated with drug users, and, most importantly, carry Narcan and learn to recognize the signs of an overdose. Overdose Awareness Day is Aug. 31. Please take the time to remember those who were lost and the grieving families they left behind. I will leave you with a quote by an unknown author to ponder: 'One community, one cause: End overdose.'
Saxon Wagner
Hayden

title: Bennet, Hickenlooper Welcome up to $1.1 billion from Inflation Reduction Act for rural electric cooperatives in Colorado
author: Staff Report
description: Colorado U.S. Senators Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper welcomed $7.3 billion from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Empowering Rural America (New ERA) program to help rural energy and…
content:
Up to $679 million will be allocated to Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association to procure renewable energy including solar, wind, and battery storage and to support the retirement of coal-fired power generation while maintaining energy reliability.
Eli Pace/Craig Press
Colorado U.S. Senators Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper welcomed $7.3 billion from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Empowering Rural America (New ERA) program to help rural energy and utility providers bring affordable, reliable clean energy to their communities across the country.
The announcement includes up to $1.16 billion for three providers in Colorado. Bennet helped secure nearly $13 billion in the I nflation Reduction Act to support rural clean energy initiatives through USDA, including the New ERA program.
The New ERA program is a $9.7 billion program created in the IRA that helps rural electric cooperatives transition to clean, affordable, and reliable energy. It is part of the largest investment in rural electrification since the New Deal. This funding includes investments for three of Colorado's rural electric cooperatives: Up to $679 million to Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association to procure renewable energy including solar, wind, and battery storage and to support the retirement of coal-fired power generation while maintaining energy reliability;
to procure renewable energy including solar, wind, and battery storage and to support the retirement of coal-fired power generation while maintaining energy reliability; $261 million to United Power to offset the cost of its transition to a strategic, clean energy portfolio; and
to offset the cost of its transition to a strategic, clean energy portfolio; and $225 million to CORE Electric Cooperative to procure renewable energy sources including wind, solar, and batteries through several power purchase agreements.
In December 2023, Bennet called on USDA to focus its awards on projects that maximize greenhouse gas emission reductions and to follow the IRA's intent to make clean energy more reliable and affordable for Americans living in rural communities.
In May 2023, Bennet joined USDA Secretary Tom Vilsack and Biden administration leaders at the White House to announce nearly $11 billion in rural clean energy grants and loan opportunities — including $9.7 billion through the New ERA program. This funding was part of the nearly $13 billion Bennet championed in the IRA to accelerate clean energy deployment, create local economic opportunities and lower costs for families in rural communities.

'Colorado's regional and municipal airports help connect communities across our state and support local economic development,' said Bennet. 'These dollars will help them invest in safety and capacity upgrades to meet Colorado's changing needs.'

The allocation will go toward rehabilitating 10,000 feet of the existing paved Taxiway A to maintain the structural integrity of the pavement and to minimize foreign object debris to extend its useful life and reconstructs the existing lighting on Taxiway A that has reached the end of its useful life.

title: Health Column: A Matter of Balance program begins Oct. 7 to help older adults prevent falls
author: Northwest Colorado Health
description: Have you or a loved one experienced a fall or have concerns about falling? Many older adults restrict themselves from activities they enjoy for fear of falling. But there are steps you can take to...
content:
Programs like Northwest Colorado Health's Aging Well Fitness Classes and the upcoming 'Matter of Balance' course can help older adults increase their activity levels and reduce the fear of falling.
Northwest Colorado Health/Courtesy photo
Have you or a loved one experienced a fall or have concerns about falling? Many older adults restrict themselves from activities they enjoy for fear of falling. But there are steps you can take to reduce your risk and prevent falls so you can continue to participate in the activities you love.
Starting on Oct. 7, Northwest Colorado Health will offer 'A Matter of Balance,' an evidence-based program designed to reduce the fear of falling and increase activity levels among older adults. The eight week class will meet weekly for two hours at the Senior Social Center through Nov. 25. This program is designed to benefit adults who are 60 or older, and are interested in improving flexibility, balance and strength.
Falls among older adults can cause serious injury or disability and they are the leading cause of injury death among those 65 and older. But falling does not need to be a normal part of aging. In addition to programs like 'A Matter of Balance,' there are simple steps you can take to protect yourself or a loved one from a fall.
Find a good balance and exercise program. There's a common misconception that muscle strength and flexibility can't be regained. While we do lose muscle as we age, exercise can partially restore strength, balance and flexibility. It's never too late to start an exercise program, especially one designed for older adults.
Talk to your health care provider. Ensure that you are taking advantage of all the preventative benefits now offered under Medicare, such as the Annual Wellness visit. Ask for a fall risk assessment and share your history of recent falls, dizziness or balance issues. Holding onto walls, furniture or someone else when walking or having difficulty walking or arising from a chair are all signs it might be time to see a physical therapist, which your health care provider can refer you to. A trained physical therapist can help improve balance and gait or provide guidance on how to use aids like a walker or cane.
Regularly review your medications. If you or a loved one is having a hard time keeping track of medicines or is experiencing side effects like dizziness, it is important to discuss this with a doctor or pharmacist and review medications each time there is a new prescription. Beware of non-prescription medications that contain sleep aids — including painkillers with 'PM' in their names. These can lead to balance issues and dizziness. Your doctor can suggest safer alternatives to reduce your risk of falling.
Get your vision and hearing checked annually. Your eyes and ears are key to keeping you on your feet. It's important to update your eyeglasses with a current prescription. Tint-changing lenses can be hazardous when going from bright sun to a darkened building. Be sure to stop and give your lenses time to adjust. Bifocals can also be problematic on stairs, so it's important to be cautious.
Keep your home safe. Many falls are caused by common hazards in the home that are easy to fix. Remove tripping hazards such as throw rugs, wires, cords and objects on the floors. Increase lighting especially at the top and bottom of the stairs. Install grab bars in the tub/shower and near the toilet, use non-skid shower mats or consider a shower chair and hand-held shower.
Talk to your family members. Enlist their support in taking these steps to stay safe. Falls are not just a seniors' issue and being open with loved ones will help keep you safe.
Northwest Colorado Health is committed to empowering all older adults to reduce their risk of falls. The Aging Well program offers evidence-based fitness classes, taught by certified instructors to help keep you safe and independent as long as possible. Our Community Health Centers accept Medicare, and offer discounted services for those who do not have insurance,ensuring quality, affordable primary care for all. Additionally, our Home Health Services are available to support physical therapy needs to assist with fall prevention when recommended by a doctor.
To learn more about these services or to sign up for 'A Matter of Balance' please call 970-871-7676 or visit NorthwestColoradoHealth.org .

title: Wolf dies after Colorado Parks and Wildlife completes capture of pack tied to livestock killings
author: Ali Ali Longwell
description: Colorado Parks and Wildlife has completed the operation to capture all six wolves from the Copper Creek Pack. Following the wolves' capture, the pack's adult male died. State officials are holding the…
content:
Pups from the Copper Creek pack are pictured in a screenshot from a video that was released by Colorado Parks and Wildlife on Monday, Aug. 19, 2024. The state says an adult male from the pack died following efforts to capture and release the animals.
Mike Usalavage/Courtesy video
Colorado Parks and Wildlife has completed the operation to capture all six wolves from the Copper Creek Pack. Following the wolves' capture, the pack's adult male died. State officials are holding the adult female and four pups in captivity before making any decisions about releasing them back into the wild.
The adult male was already injured when Parks and Wildlife captured him Friday, Aug. 30, and he had a history of preying on livestock in Grand County.
The wolf had several injuries to his right hind leg, which were unrelated to the capture, according to a press release from the agency. His body weight was 30% lower than when he was released in Colorado in December, it adds.
While the biologists administered antibiotics to the wolf for an infection related to the leg injury, he died four days later on Tuesday, Sept. 3. Parks and Wildlife will be conducting a full necropsy to determine the source of the wolf's injuries. According to the agency, it is unlikely the wolf would have survived much longer in the wild.
The adult female was captured several days earlier on Saturday, Aug. 24. The first of the pups, a male, was captured Tuesday, Sept. 3. Two more male pups were captured the next day, with the fourth and final female pup captured Thursday, Sept. 5.
This is one more wolf pup that Parks and Wildlife had previously confirmed . After the capture, the agency reported it is 'confident' there are no other pups.
Following the wolves' capture, the animals were all transported to a large enclosure — likely a wildlife sanctuary or rehabilitation center — where they can be monitored with limited human interaction. The location will not be disclosed, officials said.
Biologists from the agency were part of the capture and transport to monitor and assess the health of each of the animals.
While it can be difficult to attribute livestock deaths to specific wolves, Jeff Davis, the director of Colorado Parks and Wildlife said in an interview with the Craig Press that the agency knew the adult male was responsible for some of them.
'The male was definitely involved in livestock depredations at a time where we know (the female wolf) was in the den with pups,' Davis said. 'His destiny was more likely permanent captivity.'
The five other wolves were found to be healthy, even though the four pups are reportedly 'underweight.'
While the wolves are being held for now, Parks and Wildlife is still planning to release the wolves into the wild.
'There is no evidence that the four pups were involved in any of the livestock depredation incidents in Grand County,' reports Parks and Wildlife in a FAQ about the capture operation . 'If it is determined that the pups can thrive, (Parks and Wildlife) plans to release them when they will be adult-sized and able to hunt on their own or together in a pack.'
Davis said that its biologists expect that the pups will be fully grown around mid-November or early-December. The wolves will be collared before release.
'We're going to monitor them and promptly address any sort of conflicts if they arise with livestock,' Davis said.
Currently, the pups are still dependent on adults for food. The agency reports that they still have baby teeth and 'are not effective hunters of anything larger than a rabbit or squirrel.'
Parks and Wildlife is less clear on its plans for the adult female that has been associated with the livestock killings.
'​​If (Parks and Wildlife) decides to re-release the adult female, she will be closely monitored,' it reports.
With the Copper Creek capture and release, Davis said the ultimate goal is 'to make sure that these pups have a second chance in the wild.'
As such, whether or not the adult female is released may come down to 'what's going to give (the pups) the best chance to be successful.'
'The pups' success in the wild is elevated the more time they have with an adult — and her in particular,' Davis added.
Parks and Wildlife has yet to determine where they could be released, but it comes down to a few ​​key factors, Davis said.
'Part of that is making sure that they go into a space where they can't just run right back,' Davis said. 'The other part of that will be where we have healthy ungulate herds at that time of the year of the releases. And then where can we try to, to the best of our ability, avoid or minimize the potential conflicts with livestock producers.'
The agency has indicated that elected officials and ranchers in the release location will be notified before any releases occur.
Why Parks and Wildlife chose this course of action for the pack
Since announcing its decision to capture and relocate the wolves, Parks and Wildlife has been criticized and questioned for choosing this course of action.
For one, this contradicts recommendations and research from its 2022 wolf reintroduction and management plan . The plan states that Parks and Wildlife will not relocate wolves with depredation histories in the wild, adding that doing so is 'viewed as translocating the problem along with the wolves.'
In a statement, Davis addressed this, emphasizing that 'the plan also calls for flexibility.'
'It may not at times account for every unique situation the agency and our experts encounter,' he added.
Davis, in an interview on Monday, said that at this time when the male wolf was known to be 'really hitting livestock, that would have been a time where, according to our plan, we would consider removal.'
However, the presence of the den this spring 'made it complicated,' Davis said.
'Removing the male at that time, while he was the sole source of food and the female was denning, would likely have been fatal to the pups and counter to the restoration mandate,' Davis stated in an emailed statement.
A few things had changed by August when the agency made the decision to relocate the pack. It had previously denied a lethal action permit in July that had been requested by Middle Park stockgrowers in May. In its FAQ on the capture, Parks and Wildlife states that this denial was 'focused on events occurring between April and mid-July.'
Subsequent events — including one confirmed wolf depredation and one that was not confirmed — were what led the agency to the ultimate decision to capture the pack, Davis said.
'It's complicated in being able to point to a particular animal as the culprit of a depredation event,' he said. 'That's why we're trying to be somewhat flexible and open-minded about which one of those adults was actually involved or we think more likely was involved than not.'
Plus, the agency wanted to ensure that the pups did not grow old enough to learn this behavior from the adults.
'The ultimate goal of this whole thing is to — before they learned how to hunt and potentially be subjected to learning livestock behavior — we needed to get them out of there so that they would have a second chance in the wild to contribute to the restoration effort,' Davis said.
This does not necessarily set a precedent for future incidents as Colorado continues its reintroduction effort.
'Down the road, when we have larger packs with more adults, that would have been an entirely different decision space for us,' Davis said. 'But given that he was essentially keeping her and those pups alive, it was a difficult decision.'
One of the criticisms Parks and Wildlife has received with the Copper Creek Pack specifically, is that the male was from the Wenaha Pack in Oregon, which was connected to confirmed kills . Colorado's reintroduction plan required that wolves released in Colorado did not have a history of chronic depredation.
After the male's release in Colorado, Parks and Wildlife reported that the Wenhana Pack had not had depredations since that October — following lethal removal of four wolves from that pack — and was related to 'infrequent depredation events.'
The adult female wolf was not part of a pack and had no known history of livestock killings, according to Parks and Wildlife.
Wildlife advocacy organizations have speculated that misuse or lack of use of nonlethal actions led to these depredations.
In a letter shared by at least two wildlife advocacy nonprofits, Defenders of Wildlife and the Western Watersheds Project , Parks and Wildlife indicated that denial of a lethal take permit was done in part because producers in the area had not yet taken all courses of nonlethal mitigation available.
The letter indicates that the applicants, whose names are redacted from the letter, 'delayed using or refused to use other nonlethal techniques that could have prevented or minimized depredations.'
It later adds that 'depredations declined significantly' after the applicants later deployed some of the nonlethal measures.
Why these two wolves began killing livestock is unknown, Davis said.
'We would all be speculating as to the why. To me, I describe this as the perfect storm,' he said. 'All the other wolves that we let out in that release from Oregon, they wandered around as singles or doubles or triples, learning the landscape — understanding kind of their native prey behavior and distribution — and this particular pair just settled down right away and had pups.'
At the end of the day, however, 'this is all a behavioral issue that we're trying to address,' Davis said.
The chosen course of action 'gives us a good chance of getting in there and altering that behavior, especially for the pups,' he added.
Part of preventing future chronic depredation by wolves includes defining the term or, as Davis put it 'finalizing (Parks and Wildlife's) lethal management criteria.'
To create this criterion, the agency formed an ad-hoc working group — made up of wildlife advocates, producers and experts — earlier this year. This group will bring forth its recommendations to the Parks and Wildlife Commission in October.
The goal is to have this criterion finalized and in place before the Copper Creek animals are released, Davis said. More Like This, Tap A Topic homefeatured

title: Photos: Moffat County football vs. Berthoud
author: Andy Bockelman
description: Moffat County football moved to 1-2 with its latest game, falling 48-8 Friday against the Berthoud Spartans. The Bulldogs struggled to contain a strong offensive effort by Berthoud, facing a running…
content:
abockelman@craigdailypress.com Moffat County's Damien Lira leans in for a hit against Berthoud Friday, Sept. 6, 2024.
Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
Moffat County football moved to 1-2 with its latest game, falling 48-8 Friday against the Berthoud Spartans.
The Bulldogs struggled to contain a strong offensive effort by Berthoud, facing a running clock by halftime.
Despite the second half flying by, the Dogs were able to get themselves on the scoreboard in the final five minutes, as senior Zach Hedman broke loose for a 19-yard touchdown rush, also running in the two-point conversion.
Hedman has averaged triple-digit yardage in MoCo's first three games, rushing for exactly 100 yards against the Spartans.
'It felt good to score like that,' Hedman said. 'They came out to win and we fell short. I think we need to get our energy up out there.'
The Bulldogs' next matchup is on the road with the Grand Valley Cardinals on Sept. 20, a game sandwiched by two bye weeks, leading up to league play in October.
MCHS head coach Nick Colgate said the extra prep time will help players worry less about competition and more about improving the flow of the game, especially those who are still adjusting to the varsity level.
'Overall, we're seeing those improvements each week, but we really need to do the little things right and go from there,' he said. 'I think with almost two weeks to get ready, we'll see a huge jump in how our kids perform.' title: Lance Scranton: Complicaitons or complexities?
author: Lance Scranton
description: Take a deep dive into the various state of affairs in our country and you will get confused and bewildered! Reading keeps you sharp but writing down your thoughts compels your attention in a much...
content:
Take a deep dive into the various state of affairs in our country and you will get confused and bewildered! Reading keeps you sharp but writing down your thoughts compels your attention in a much different direction knowing that people and cultures can understand complicated ideas because there is usually an answer that is fairly straightforward. But complex problems are difficult to manage because the unknowns are very difficult to manage or control.
Our streets can be complicated especially if you are unfamiliar and get lost. But if you get access to a map or someone gives you directions you'll find your destination. If you find yourself trying to manage a subway system in New York City you might have a more difficult time because of the complexities involved in just about every decision you make about scheduling the trains. The complicated and complex require very different approaches and demand more acceptance of variability.
What seems to be happening in our culture is the propensity for well-meaning, intelligent people to apply complicated solutions to complex problems. It isn't that the problem is unsolvable; it's just that the answer might involve an acceptance of other variations that haven't been considered or that the outcome or causes might not be as straightforward as we think.
People are complex and if we apply a complicated solution to a complex issue; we're going to run into frustrations. The social sciences have certainly contributed to the idea that if we simply apply a set of prescribed answers to many of our problems they will be solved. Often when we say that a problem is complex people think that you are making an excuse for some infraction or feeling sorry for the wrong person. Sure, that could be the reason but it could also be that answers to a complicated problem won't be sufficient for a complex problem.
Over the past few years the mental health of our children has become a major point of emphasis in our schools and there are many programs being implemented that are designed to impact the well being of young people. But, again, humans are complex and it astounds me that so often in our public schools we believe that throwing a program at children will be enough of an intervention to make the most beneficial difference. I am certain that the school that suffered the latest horrific school shooting had programs in place to help mitigate student mental health. Surely people involved in the school's administrative services were aware of some of the issues surrounding the perpetrator's mental health.
But here is where the complexity shows up: What if they didn't? What if despite our best efforts people decide that they are going to do things that bewilder our common sense? Do we understand that mental health is affected by more than a program? What about the other complex aspects of human development and mental health that we are hesitant to address? Social media, societal expectations, healthy eating and nutrition, family life and spiritual traditions all have a huge impact on the mental health of a child (and of an adult).
Too often we avoid these conversations in the name of privacy rights and personal freedom but we know that our diet plays a huge role in our well being and societal expectation are markers of our values as a culture, social media is negatively impacting the healthy mental development of children and the spiritual component of our lives leads to a more unselfish and less self-centered view of ourselves.
We know this is a complex issue that will require an approach that goes beyond the complicated. We won't always be successful but we understand that complexity demands a different standard than what we are doing as a culture right now. We all see it, we recognize it even though we might have trouble making an accurate description of the problem but we all see the edges of our culture that are fraying and we know we need to do something about it and the solution starts with understanding the complex nature of that which faces us as a culture and being willing to be a part of the solution. More on that in two weeks.

title: Moffat County 4-H shooters show their skills
author: Andy Bockelman
description: Marksmanship means a lot in Moffat County, and young competitors with the local 4-H shooting sports programs were on target in recent weeks. Moffat County took multiple honors during the Colorado…
content:
The Moffat County shotgun team has their gear ready to go as part of the 4-H Shooting Sports State Championships.
Courtesy Photo
Marksmanship means a lot in Moffat County, and young competitors with the local 4-H shooting sports programs were on target in recent weeks.
Moffat County took multiple honors during the Colorado State Championships hosted across multiple weekends in Pueblo and Colorado Springs.
As part of the first wave of events on Aug. 17 and 18 in Pueblo, Travis LeFevre took first place honors in the scope category of the .22 rifle competition, winning by just a little more than a single point.
'It's a lot of precision in that one,' he said of the scope event. 'A little bit of adjustment matters in points, it makes a big difference.'
The Moffat County senior also took sixth in the air rifle event, though his full standings in the .22 saw him at eighth altogether in cumulative scoring.
LeFerve and teammate Jamison Fehringer also took fourth in the group count for senior air rifle utility. Moffat County's Travis LeFevre joins fellow rifle shooters for an award ceremony at the 4-H Shooting Sports State Championships. Courtesy Photo
While he didn't yet qualify to join the Colorado rifle team at nationals next summer — in his last year of eligibility for that event — it's entirely possible LeFevre could be going to that level if some shooters are unable to go.
'There's a lot of the same kids in some stuff, and they can't go for every event, so I'll just have to wait to hear,' he said.
Another Moffat County firearm aficionado who stood out in one particular discipline was Daniel Gomez in the shotgun competition during Labor Day weekend in Colorado Springs.
Gomez was tied for the lead in the trap competition, only to fall to reserve champion after a shoot-off round that didn't go his way. Moffat County's Daniel Gomez displays ribbons won as part of the 4-H Shooting Sports State Championships. Courtesy Photo
Still, the MCHS sophomore was pretty pleased with his rounds overall, with trap his clear specialty.
'I had good focus and fundamentals and was really zoned in for that,' he said.
Gomez's proficiency with a shotgun has seen him compete in multiple American Trap Association events at home and across the state, though his goal is to improve a bit in the other components of shotgun shooting, skeet and sporting clays.
'I did better in them than last year, but I still want to get better,' he said.
Moffat County teams saw stronger results as a collective than in the solo rankings, such as the senior compound limited archery squad comprised of Kadynce Hampton, Malykai Hampton, Connor Nagel, Zayne St. Martin and Devren Styles. The junior compound unlimited team took sixth, including Gunner Hampton, Logan Nagel, Gunner Pepping and Annie Woodworth.
Austin Jazwick finished fifth in the junior 3P rifle category in both individual and team standings, while Owen Jazwick and Teagan Siminoe took eighth in multiple junior air rifle events. As the only member of the .22 air pistol team, Adylee St. Martin was 12th.
The senior shotgun team finished as reserve champs in the trap category, with a score of 190 — only one tally behind the Weld County group. The senior team includes Gomez, Tristen Counts, Stone Balleck, Zach Winters, Wyatt Dade and Cody Dade.
The group took fifth in clays and sixth in skeet.
The weekend was an exhausting one for Cody Dade, who noted it involved a late-night drive after the Moffat County football game against Steamboat.
'I didn't sleep at all that night,' he said. 'We got there around 4 (a.m.) and were shooting at 7, so I tried to just sleep in the truck since there was no point getting a hotel room for three hours.'
He noted that having a good team rapport is helpful; though they all shoot individually, they still support each other.
'It's great to hang out with my brother one last time like that,' Cody said. 'It's also cool having a lot of other football players on the team because we just have a bond we don't have with anyone else.'
