title: Not opposed to shooting predators, former Routt County rancher speaks out against Wyoming wolf killing
author: Trevor Ballantyne
description: Born and raised on a Cherokee reservation in North Carolina, Grey Bear owned Sleeping Giant Ranch in Routt County from 2002 to 2017 and now owns a hunting and fishing lodge in the British Columbia,…
content:
Born and raised on a Cherokee reservation in North Carolina, Grey Bear owned Sleeping Giant Ranch in Routt County from 2002 to 2017 and now owns a hunting and fishing lodge in the British Columbia , Canada.
, Canada. The Canadian province, larger than the countries of France and Germany combined, is a place where wildlife officials estimate there to be a population of roughly 8,500 grey wolves.
Over the phone Thursday, Grey Bear said the wolves have taken on average 1.5 horses per year from his property in north-central British Columbia and, on occasions where he has caught wolves in the act, he has killed the predators.
It happened as recently as last year when he returned to his ranch to find a mother wolf and three juveniles cornering a mare and a foal in a round pen outside his house, he recalled.
Without a gun handy, the former Routt County resident used his hickory wood cane to strike one of the juvenile wolves over its head, stunning the animal into submission before it retreated to the mother wolf.
At the same time, Grey Bear said his dog, a German shepherd and trained service dog, went about snapping the neck of one of one of the other young wolves, killing the wolf instantly.
'The other wolf pup got away,' Grey Bear said. 'I had a dead foal laying there. I had a mare whose right inside hind knee was ripped open — still has a bad scar there. I had a couple yearling stud colts in there that had bite marks on their feet and their hips, and then I had a mare that had bite marks and rips on her throat.'
Grey Bear said he grabbed a gun from his house and 'finished off' the young wolf he had hit with his cane. The mother wolf and the other young wolf ran off, but the rancher said he knew they would be back and spent the rest of the night and the next day 'with a rifle and a spotlight just waiting.'
The wolves eventually did return, and he shot them.
'The alpha wolf, the male, was pretty smart and he stayed back just on the edge of the woods and I could see him … but I never could get a shot at him for the first three days so I took the momma wolf and all the pups over there and put 'em in a pile,' Grey Bear recounted.
'I waited and it took me three days, and finally he went out and got his nerve up and got brave enough to go over there and start sniffing, and that was the last thing he would ever smell. I got rid of the whole pack,' he added. 'That was a situation.'
Grey Bear, almost two thousand miles away and speaking from a landline at his Grey Bear Ranch and Lodge in north-central British Columbia, still follows news from Northwest Colorado. He has killed wolves before and is admittedly, and deeply, opposed to the wolf reintroduction effort underway in the state.
in north-central British Columbia, still follows news from Northwest Colorado. He has killed wolves before and is admittedly, and deeply, opposed to the wolf reintroduction effort underway in the state. The state's grey wolf reintroduction program was approved by voters in 2020, and Colorado Parks and Wildlife worked with wildlife officials in Oregon to begin relocating 10 wolves to the state in December.
Since then, CPW has acknowledged at least seven reported wolf depredation events in April , and said one of the reintroduced wolves died of natural causes.
, and said one of the reintroduced wolves died of natural causes. But make no mistake: Grey Bear does not in any way support how a Wyoming man acted in February after running down a juvenile grey wolf with his snowmobile before deciding to muzzle the animal and parade it around a local bar in the town of Daniel before killing it later that evening.
before deciding to muzzle the animal and parade it around a local bar in the town of Daniel before killing it later that evening. The February incident, first reported by WyoFile.com , became national news and prompted global outrage and wildlife advocates to push for a tourism boycott for the entire state of Wyoming.
, became national news and prompted global outrage and wildlife advocates to push for a tourism boycott for the entire state of Wyoming. Wolves can be killed at any time and without justification in zones encompassing roughly 85% of Wyoming, a state with the least restrictive laws for predator kills.
Wyoming wildlife authorities eventually issued a citation to the man, Cody Roberts, charging him with a misdemeanor violation of possessing live wildlife and issuing a $250 fine .
. The Sublette County Sheriff's Office has since launched its own investigation into Roberts for potential felony charges of animal cruelty. The investigation is ongoing.
Grey Bear is a rancher, a man who has not only killed wolves but also other predators, including a grizzly bear that he dispatched with a pipe after finding it attacking his horses. But he has signed a petition to implore authorities to charge Roberts with animal cruelty .
. 'It is not that I am against the taking of predators; I am just absolutely and totally against the cruelty that was exhibited by this idiot,' Grey Bear said. 'What he did is within the balance of the law as far as taking the wolf down. If he dispatched the wolf immediately, there would have been nothing said about it, but to do what he did after running it over, that is just unconscionable, that is not human. That is just wrong.'

The Colorado General Assembly just adjourned our annual 120-day legislative session. As we concluded our work, spirits were high as several major bipartisan efforts successfully passed , including a permanent solution for slowing the growth in property taxes , modernizing our school funding formula , protecting thousands of acres of wetlands and so much more.

Further, the partisan rancor that often led headlines last year was significantly reduced this year, and Colorado will be better for it as we worked together to deliver much-needed solutions and progress on some of our state's most pressing challenges. For me, responding to the needs of the rural and mountain communities I serve in the State Senate had me working with colleagues on both sides of the aisle and always focusing on results — and we got a lot of good done.
Addressing the rising cost of living in Colorado was top of mind this session. To that end, we cut income taxes, reduced sales taxes and made it easier for working families, parents, educators, healthcare professionals and many others to get ahead. title: Flag sponsorships available through Rotary Club of Craig
author: Staff Report
description: The Rotary Club of Craig is offering community members the opportunity to put their patriotism on display. This year marks the 18th year of the Rotary Club's American flag project, and the club is…
content:
The Rotary Club of Craig is offering community members the opportunity to put their patriotism on display.
This year marks the 18th year of the Rotary Club's American flag project, and the club is asking businesses and community members to sponsor flags that will be displayed throughout town during the year. The flags will be displayed on holidays including Memorial Day, Flag Day, the Fourth of July, Colorado Day, Patriot Day, Columbus/Indigenous Peoples' Day and Veterans Day.
On Yampa Avenue, the flags will be placed on the light poles on both sides of the street from Fourth Street to Sixth Street. The flags will be left up from May 30-Nov. 11 and replaced as needed.
On Victory Way, the flags will be placed on both sides of the street starting at Lincoln Street and heading west every 100 feet to Finley Lane. Flags may be placed on a shorter section of Victory Way as requested for additional events throughout the year.
Flags are not placed for winter holidays due to safety concerns. Altogether, 231 flags were sponsored this past year and the club is hoping to have even more sponsors this year.
Rotarian Randy Looper shared that, in addition to being a source of local pride and downtown beautification, the flag display can also provide 'a great way to impress visitors driving through the area.'
The price to purchase a flag sponsorship is $85 per flag per year. There is no limit to the number of flags that can be purchased. All sponsors will be recognized at the beginning and end of the club's flag year.
Purchase forms are available via the Rotary Club. The completed form, along with sponsorship checks, can be returned or mailed to the the Craig Rotary Club, P.O. Box 1400, Craig, CO 81625. Questions can be directed to Dorina Fredrickson at 970-629-1089 or Randy Looper at 970-629-0654. Fredrickson can also be reached via email at craigrotaryclub@gmail.com .

title: Moffat County golfer Arianna Anderson shoots 219 at two-day state tourney
author: Andy Bockelman
description: At the highest level of play, Moffat County golfer Arianna Anderson has seen some tricky conditions. But she also knows the more difficult the links, the better she will be down the road. Anderson…
content:
Moffat County's Arianna Anderson smiles from behind the wheel of a golf cart at Yampa Valley Golf Course. Anderson shot a 219 during the two-day 3A state championships on May 20-21 in Loveland.
Andy Bockelman/Craig Press At the highest level of play, Moffat County golfer Arianna Anderson has seen some tricky conditions. But she also knows the more difficult the links, the better she will be down the road.
Anderson placed 65th during the 3A CHSAA State Championships at The Olde Course in Loveland, shooting a 109 on the first day and 110 the second.
The Front Range location was one MCHS coach Tim Adams said was one of the best he's seen since heading the program.
'Of all the courses that the girls have played on for state, that's probably the best one. It's really fair, really neat, I like it a lot. It's a more traditional course, a familiar feel, easy to walk.'
Anderson's game was helped along by the layout, which wasn't at all formidable from the tee box.
'There were a lot of straight shots, pretty easy to get on the fairway, and the whole course was pretty straight,' Anderson said. 'The drives were kind of what saved me the first day.'
However, the Loveland course had another feature that made things more difficult.
'She had a little trouble with the greens,' Adams said. 'They were really fast. Sometimes when I say that, I think what I mean is they're actually normal. We're just not used to that, because our greens are so slow, and we go anywhere and that's kind of a shock.'
Putting was hard for nearly the entire field of golfers.
'It was hard to read, and everybody I was playing with was having issues with that,' Anderson said. 'They couldn't read the speed or tell where it would go. The course itself was pretty mildly hard, but the greens were really hard.'
It wasn't just the act of tapping the ball in the hole, Adams added, but also the shots leading up to that.
'She had a hard time holding the green; she'd be 100 yards out and hit a pretty nice approach shot and just would always roll off the back of the green,' Adams said. 'She wasn't the only one; a lot of kids were struggling with that. She doesn't hit her ball with a lot of spin on it, so that part was tough.'
With only one stroke difference between rounds, the second year at the state level was far better overall for Anderson than last year, when she shot a 108 in Aspen before a 123 the next day.
She noted it was easier to concentrate this time around.
'Things going on outside of golf can mess with your head sometimes, but I still played pretty well,' Anderson said. 'The girls I played with were super nice, and it was still a good time. I was able to get some confidence going two years in a row, but I don't think I'm up there with the girls who were in the top 20. I still have more practicing to do, and I'm right in the middle of it right now. I'm happy with it, but I can definitely do better. At the end of the day, it's just high school golf, and if you take it so seriously, it's not fun, then there's no point in doing it.'
Anderson is a home-school student nearly done with her senior year and will be working at Yampa Valley Golf Course this summer. She is considering pursuing college golf, though her academics will be the priority.
She added that getting more involved in the sport has been beneficial to her in numerous aspects.
'It was a really good experience in general. It taught me how to handle mental stuff in a good way. I really enjoyed the people I got to be friends with; I think those friendships will last.'

title: United Way gifted large donation for financial literacy program
author: Staff Report
description: United Way of the Yampa Valley recently announced a donation of $25,000 from the Wells Fargo Foundation in support of United Way's Women United Financial Literacy Program. According to United Way, the…
content:
United Way of the Yampa Valley recently announced a donation of $25,000 from the Wells Fargo Foundation in support of United Way's Women United Financial Literacy Program. According to United Way, the contribution be used to 'further empower individuals in our community to take control of their financial futures.'
The Financial Literacy Program, managed by the affiliate group, Women United, is dedicated to providing essential financial education to those in need. The program offers a comprehensive range of courses designed to equip participants with the knowledge and skills necessary for financial success.
The curriculum includes foundational courses such as Budgeting 101, Credit 101, Homebuying 101 and Investing 101. Each course, comprised of three classes, covers essential topics and practical strategies to help individuals manage their finances effectively for a minimal fee. The overall aim of the courses is to help participants make informed financial decisions and build a more secure future for themselves and their families.
'We are immensely grateful to the Wells Fargo Foundation for their continued support of our financial literacy program,' said Kate Nowak, Executive Director of United Way of the Yampa Valley. 'Their partnership allows us to expand our reach and make a meaningful difference in the lives of individuals throughout our community.'
For more information about United Way of the Yampa Valley's Women United Financial Literacy Program and how to get involved, visit UnitedWayoftheYampaValley.org .

title: Obituary: Nancy Jo Hettinger
description: December 11, 1938 – May 7, 2024 Nancy was born and raised in Tama, Iowa to parents Merle and Trudie (Warner) Kensinger. She graduated from Tama, Iowa in 1957 and attended the University of Iowa,...
content:
Obituaries Obituaries | May 22, 2024 Nancy Jo Hettinger
Provided Photo December 11, 1938 – May 7, 2024 Nancy was born and raised in Tama, Iowa to parents Merle and Trudie (Warner) Kensinger. She graduated from Tama, Iowa in 1957 and attended the University of Iowa, studying Arts. In 1960, she married Kenton Jens and they had three daughters; Kelley, Kathy and Kristen. In 1972, the family moved to Colorado where they settled and loved the mountains. Nancy enjoyed working as an Ad Designer at the Craig Daily Press. title: MCSD Whiteboard: District Accountability Committee tackles big issues
author: Moffat County School District
description: The Moffat County School District DAC, or District Accountability Committee, was back in session last week. It's been a while, and there was a lot to discuss. The DAC includes teachers, parents and…
content:
The Moffat County School District DAC, or District Accountability Committee, was back in session last week. It's been a while, and there was a lot to discuss.
The DAC includes teachers, parents and community representation. On Wednesday, the DAC reviewed what the district has been up to this spring semester. A laundry list of progress was discussed. It was gratifying to hear that teachers are feeling much better and more secure in their positions after the work that's been done to improve transparency and communication, systems and procedures, and support for educators across the board.
There were also some important concerns voiced by parents, which the district is grateful to hear. The district is committed to building toward a consistently excellent education, provided to each and every student, and we learned about places we can improve. There's a ton of work to do. The good news is we think we've laid the groundwork to make major strides in the near future.
The DAC also discussed the 2024-25 soon-to-be-proposed district budget. The Board of Education and the public will review the budget in the coming weeks, but the district was looking for DAC input as the budget nears finalization for board approval.
There was plenty of learning gleaned from this discussion. Some strategies will be reviewed following this feedback, and others were confirmed to be on the right track. The nearly completed budget proposal will include enhancements to several sectors of the district's operations, including a capital infusion, a historic boost in compensation for teachers, staff and administration and an investment in curriculum and professional development.
This is how the district is putting its money where its mouth is. We need more great teachers, more veteran teachers, more certified teachers and more well-trained teachers. We know that's what we need to provide a great education to our students. We're getting there. It might take some time, but we believe we're on the right track.
There was a discussion as well about the capital plan for the next five years. The district has a plan that can be funded by our current available funding, but the reality is — as was discussed in DAC — there is a much greater need than we can fulfill with our own funding. We're looking to BEST grants and other capital funding sources to maximize our capacity, but we're going to need more help. The DAC is an important first conversation to have as that process moves forward over the next several years. Our facilities are aging and out of date, and desperately need maintenance and updating. That will have to happen soon.
The bottom line is we're trying to build a district we can all be proud of, and proud to send our kids to. We are working hard to make that true. We have work to do. We're grateful for community support, including the DAC, as we seek to roll up our sleeves and get the job done.

title: School board looks to fill immediate vacancy
author: Staff Report
description: The Board of Education for Moffat County School District is accepting applications from persons interested in serving on the school board for District E. The selected candidate will serve from the…
content:
The Board of Education for Moffat County School District is accepting applications from persons interested in serving on the school board for District E. The selected candidate will serve from the date of appointment in June 2024 until the next regular biennial school year election in November 2025. The board's current District E representative, Laura Woodworth, will be vacating her seat due to a move outside of the district's boundary lines. To be eligible for appoint, a candidate must be a registered elector of the school district for at least 12 consecutive months prior to the date of appointment, be a resident of the director district in which the vacancy exists, and have never been convicted of a of a sexual offense against a child. Any person who meets the qualifications and who would like to be considered for the appointment is invited to file a written notice of such intention by June 17 at the office of the Superintendent of Schools, located at 600 Texas Ave. in Craig. Following receipt of the written notice of intent, qualified candidates will receive a list of questions. The board will interview prospective candidates at a public meeting on June 24. For further information, contact Taylor Smith at 970-826-6261. A map defining District E can be found by visiting the Board of Education's page on the Moffat County School District website. content:
Obituaries Obituaries | Jun 5, 2024 R. Thomas Kirby
Provided Photo December 7, 1960 – May 15, 2024 R. Thomas Kirby, known to friends and family as Tom, passed away on May 15, 2024, at the age of 63. Tom was born on December 7, 1960. He was a dedicated IT Manager at Swift Communications, a position in which he took great pride and excelled for many years. Tom moved to the Vail Valley in 2008, where he embraced the beauty of the mountains and the vibrant community. In 2018, he relocated to Rifle, Colorado, continuing to build lasting relationships and cherished memories. Tom leaves behind his heartbroken Colorado family, including his cherished partner of 17 years, Keri Lamle, and her children Luke, David, and Meghan Lamle. He also leaves an extensive community of friends and colleagues who will remember him for his kindness, dedication, and warm spirit. The family would like to invite those who were touched by Tom's spark of life to join them on June 15, 2024, at 2 pm, at the Miller Ranch Community Center (25 Mill Loft Street, Edwards, Colorado 81632) for a Moment to Remember a Remarkable Man. Tom's legacy is one of love, friendship, and unwavering support for those around him. His memory will live on in the hearts of all who knew him. title: Pork producers looking for candidates with the chops to serve on state council
author: Staff Report
description: The Colorado Pork Producers Council is seeking candidates to run for vacant positions on its board of directors. The election will be held June 25 at the council's annual meeting in La Junta. To be…
content:
The Colorado Pork Producers Council is seeking candidates to run for vacant positions on its board of directors. The election will be held June 25 at the council's annual meeting in La Junta. To be eligible to run, candidates must be an owner/operator, upper management employee, contract grower, former producer or allied industry (member) in the pork industry. This includes any person who is actively engaged in the pork industry as the actual owner/operator of a pig farming enterprise; an employee in an upper management/supervisory position of a pig farming enterprise; a contract feeder/grower/ farrower of pigs; a person formerly engaged in pork production in Colorado less than 10 years ago as an owner/ operator or as a contract grower/ feeder/ farrower; or a person actively engaged in the pork industry within the state of Colorado and affiliated with a business or academic institution that provides a product or service to pig producers. Any person who is a current participant in the Colorado Pork industry and meets this criteria is eligible to run. Board terms begin Jan. 1, 2025. Additional information about the Colorado Pork Producers Council can be found at CoPork.org . For questions about the council or running for a board seat, or to RSVP to attend the meeting, contact the council's office at (970)356-4964 or info@copork.org . title: Local landowners, ag producers can take advantage of USDA conservation programs
author: Staff Report
description: The U.S. Department of Agriculture is now accepting applications from agricultural producers and private landowners up for the department's Grassland Conservation Reserve Program with the signup…
content:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is now accepting applications from agricultural producers and private landowners up for the department's Grassland Conservation Reserve Program with the signup window open through June 28.
According to the agency, the program offered by the USDA's Farm Service Agency is a voluntary working lands conservation program that enables participants to conserve grasslands and provide conservation benefits for wildlife, soil health and carbon sequestration, while still continuing most grazing and haying practices.
More than 2.3 million acres from agricultural producers and private landowners were accepted through the 2023 Grassland Conservation Reserve Program signup. The current program participation includes 8.64 million acres, which is part of the 24.8 million acres enrolled in Conservation Reserve Program opportunities overall.
In late 2023, President Joe Biden signed legislation extending the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018, more commonly known as the 2018 Farm Bill, through Sept. 30. This extension allows authorized programs, including the Conservation Reserve Program, to continue operating.
Moffat County landowners and producers interested in the program can contact the local U.S. Department of Agriculture Service Center at 970-824-3476 to learn more or apply for the program before the deadline.
Applications for Continuous CRP signup are also being accepted at Bit.ly/3RjlMiV .

The Farm Service Agency also offers financial assistance to producers and landowners enrolled in the Conservation Reserve Program to improve the health of their forests through the Forest Management Incentive , which can help participants with forest management practices such as brush management and prescribed burning.

title: Meghan Lukens: Breakthrough legislative session
author: Meghan Lukens
description: Two years ago, you elected me to serve in the Colorado State House and stand up for Northwest Colorado. From Vail to Rangely, Oak Creek to Maybell, I continue to keep my commitment to the...
content:
Meghan Lukens
Legislative Update Two years ago, you elected me to serve in the Colorado State House and stand up for Northwest Colorado. From Vail to Rangely, Oak Creek to Maybell, I continue to keep my commitment to the people of House District 26 to deliver on the three Es: education, the environment and the economy. I continued my work from last year to accomplish these goals and delivered real results for Colorado this 2024 Legislative Session. As a social studies teacher, it is critical that we give every student the resources they need to succeed. One of the reasons I ran for the Colorado House of Representatives was to eliminate the Budget Stabilization Factor, and I am proud to say that this legislative session, we successfully eliminated the BSF. This commitment to our students and their future means that starting next year, our schools will have an additional $560 million to provide students individualized attention with smaller class sizes, pay our hardworking teachers what they deserve, and ensure that everyone is given the resources they need for the best learning environment. This commitment continues to our rural schools. For the first time, we created an ongoing rural school funding stream through a new 'Rural Factor' within the School Finance Act. This adds almost $36 million for rural students' success. In 2025, the State is committing an additional $225 million to the over 132,000 rural and remote students in Colorado, who will now have the adequate resources they deserve. I also supported landmark legislation that will make it easier and more affordable for students to attend college. Students and families making under $90,000 will soon be eligible for a tax credit that will cover the full cost of community college, or two years of a four-year degree. We also capped tuition increases at state universities to save families money. On the Western Slope, we know how vital our water is to survival. I am proud to report that legislators are serious about protecting this precious resource. As the snow melts and the water flows, we passed HB24-1379, which restores critical protections for Colorado's streams, rivers and wetlands. The State House and Senate unanimously passed SB24-197, Water Conservation Measures, which will implement recommendations from the Colorado River Drought Task Force to protect Colorado's water supply. In order to maximize the water flowing through our homes, I sponsored HB24-1362, a bipartisan bill to promote conserving graywater through water reuse in residential buildings. Economic Prosperity Our working families are the backbone of the Western Slope from our teachers to our agriculturalsmall business owners. This legislative session, there was strong bipartisan support to uplift theeconomy and support our families. I am proud that all of my bills boosting rural prosperitypassed both the House and Senate and have been signed into law by Governor Polis. These billsboost our rural and agriculture economies, making it easier for folks to enter fast growingindustries, and helping parents access affordable childcare.We also worked hard to make it more affordable to live in Colorado. We passed bipartisanlegislation to reduce property taxes for homeowners and businesses. We also made the seniorhomestead property tax exemption portable so older Coloradans can downsize and save money ifthey want to without losing this tax break. Finally we extended tax breaks for senior housingcosts, cut income taxes, and boosted tax credits for agriculture and businesses that hire in rural areas.

title: Obituary: Rex Polen
description: April 12, 1954 – May 18, 2024 Rex Polen, a man cherished by all who knew him, passed away leaving a legacy of love and generosity. Born on April 12, 1954, to Forest Leon Polen...
content:
Obituaries Obituaries | Jun 12, 2024 Rex Polen
Provided Photo April 12, 1954 – May 18, 2024 Rex Polen, a man cherished by all who knew him, passed away leaving a legacy of love and generosity. Born on April 12, 1954, to Forest Leon Polen and Geneva Bassett, Rex's life was marked by his selfless nature and his willingness to help anyone in need, often offering the very shirt off his back. Rex attended high school in Grants, New Mexico. In 1995, he married Dorothy Harrell at the Routt County Courthouse in Steamboat Springs, CO. Together, they built a life filled with love and hard work, owning and operating the Western American Drilling Company. Rex also worked as a driver for Axis Steele, displaying his strong work ethic and dedication. Outside of his professional life, Rex embraced the roles of a cowboy and carpenter. He found joy in these pursuits, often accompanied by his beloved dogs Duke, Daisy, and Annabelle. However, his greatest pleasure was spending time with his grandchildren, cherishing every moment with them. Rex is survived by his loving wife, Dorothy Polen, and his son, Paul Harrell (LeAnne). He leaves behind his cherished grandchildren: Raine, Myla, Aida, and Ryan. His memory will also live on through his sisters, Rita Henry and Renne Arrvda, his half-brother Perry Sanchez, and half-sister Deborah Cervantes. He will be fondly remembered by his niece Delanie and her children: Trinitie Beckner (Everlie Kassees), Michael 'Bubba' Thompson, Charisma Delgado, and Justice McMillan. A celebration of Rex's life will be held on Saturday, June 29, 2024, at 2:00 PM at the Polen home in Craig, CO. Friends and family are invited to join in remembering and honoring a man whose love and kindness touched so many lives.

title: Health column: Prevention is key to men's health
author: Northwest Colorado Health
description: Just as preventative maintenance is important for our vehicles, bikes and skis, regular check-ups and age-appropriate prevention screenings are key to staying healthy, preventing disease and avoiding…
content:
June is Men's Health Month, designated to heighten awareness of preventable health problems and encourage early detection and treatment of disease among men and boys.
Northwest Colorado Health/Courtesy photo Just as preventative maintenance is important for our vehicles, bikes and skis, regular check-ups and age-appropriate prevention screenings are key to staying healthy, preventing disease and avoiding costly health complications later in life.
Research has shown that men die at higher rates for nine of the top ten causes of death, including heart disease, cancer, diabetes and suicide. Because men are more likely to have poor health habits, and less likely to seek regular medical attention, men are dying about five years sooner than women are.
But it doesn't have to be this way. According to Men's Health Network, more than half of premature deaths among men are preventable. Men can live longer and healthier by getting regular medical checkups.
June is Men's Health Month, designated to heighten awareness of preventable health problems and encourage early detection and treatment of disease among men and boys.
Important factors influencing men's health include a lack of health insurance and too few visits to medical providers for check ups and health screenings.
Financial limitations do not have to be a barrier to good health. Northwest Colorado Health's Community Health Centers in Steamboat Springs and Craig offer the following preventative health services benefitting men. Services are offered on a sliding fee scale based on income, and are available in English and Spanish.
Review your overall health status and discuss your concerns with a medical provider. Men 39 and younger should get a physical exam every 2-3 years; men 40 to 49 every two years; and men 50 and older should get annual physical exams. Your provider will also discuss your risk and screening options for common cancers, such as prostate, skin and colon cancer, which have a greater chance of successful treatment when found early. We also offer DOT physicals.
Cardiovascular screenings involve a blood pressure check and simple finger prick, which should be done yearly regardless of age. Within 20 minutes, patients learn their cholesterol panel – LDL ('bad' cholesterol), HDL ('good' cholesterol) and triglyceride levels. The test also reveals a person's blood glucose level, a good indicator of diabetes risk. Follow-up sessions are available to create a personalized health improvement plan to help assist with small changes that can have a big impact on overall health. This service is available at no cost. To make an appointment, call 970-871-7692 in Craig or 970-871-7694 in Steamboat Springs.
Testing for STIs, including HIV, gonorrhea, syphilis and herpes simplex virus (HSV) is available on a sliding fee scale for uninsured patients. Individuals of all ages can make a confidential appointment with one of our health care providers to discuss sexual health and family planning.
Physical and emotional health are connected, and our thoughts, feelings and actions can affect our physical health. Our behavioral health providers help patients struggling with chronic medical conditions, stress, depression, anxiety, substance abuse, sleeping problems and weight management.
Take control of your health. Make an appointment for any of the above services by calling Northwest Colorado Health at 970-824-8233 in Craig or 970-879-1632 in Steamboat Springs.
Visit northwestcoloradohealth.org for more information.

title: Moffat County workers can benefit from new state paid leave resource
author: Ashley Dishman
description: Officials with the Department of Labor and Employment are reminding Moffat County residents about a new resource that offers paid leave for workers. Colorado's Family and Medical Leave Insurance…
content:
Officials with the Department of Labor and Employment are reminding Moffat County residents about a new resource that offers paid leave for workers.
Colorado's Family and Medical Leave Insurance program, created by a vote in 2020, gives workers partial pay replacement when serious life events force employees to temporarily step away from the job. Workers and employers contribute premiums to fund the program.
FAMLI leave can be used for life events such as welcoming a new child, managing a serious health condition or caring for a loved one with a serious health condition.
Colorado is the first state to set up a paid-leave program through a public vote instead of through the legislative branch. Workers with approved claims can choose to get their payments directly to a bank account or on a reloading debit card.
Kirsten Nichols with the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment shared, 'We especially want to make sure that Colorado's rural workers know about FAMLI.'
'As you may know, rural workers are far less likely than their urban and suburban counterparts to have access to employer-sponsored leave or even unpaid time off when facing a medical condition. At the same time, rural residents must travel farther distances for health care.'
More than 100 workers in Craig and the Moffat County area have taken advantage of Colorado's new paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance since the program began in January, according to data from the state Department of Labor and Employment.
The most common reason claimants in Craig and Moffat County took leave was to care for their own serious health condition (72 claims). The next most common leave type was to bond with a new child (23 claims).
FAMLI benefits are calculated on a sliding scale using the individual's average weekly wage from the previous five calendar quarters in relation to the average weekly wage for the state of Colorado. Workers can check their potential benefit payments with an online Premium and Benefits calculator .
. So far Colorado has paid more than $243 million in wage replacement to workers facing life events that force them to temporarily step away from work. Additional statewide claims details are available online at the FAMLI By The Numbers page.
page. Additional information about the FAMLI program can be found by visiting Famli.Colorado.gov or calling (866)263-2654 [(866)-CO-FAMLI] from 7 a.m. – 6 p.m. Monday – Friday.

A young woman going for a walk with her elderly mother in the garden.
Shelli Steele/Courtesy photo Bones are made of living tissue, and like all the other living tissue in our bodies, they change as our health changes and as we age.
Memorial Regional Health's new board-certified Family Nurse Practitioner, Bridget Mucha, is an orthopedics and bone health specialist. She'll be holding regular clinic hours at MRH to help patients assess, treat and monitor bone health issues such as osteoporosis.
'Many members of Craig's community are physically active, whether it's with their line of work or their activities,' Mucha said, 'and we should absolutely be checking bone health regularly to ensure that fractures can be prevented before they happen. Fractures are debilitating and can lead to the loss of independence and mobility and ultimately decrease a patient's quality of life. Confidence in your body is important, and I want my patients to have confidence in their bodies' ability to continue to do the things they love.'
If your bones have low mass, you may be diagnosed with osteopenia. People who are slender and active have osteopenia, but may also be healthy with strong bones. In other words, osteopenia isn't necessarily bad. But in less active and older people, osteopenia can be a precursor to osteoporosis, which literally means 'porous bone.'
Osteoporosis is common, but rarely has visible symptoms. Women are more at risk for a fracture than breast cancer, and men are more at risk for a fracture than prostate cancer.
Because osteoporosis isn't something we can see or feel from the outside, it's common for people to be unaware they have it until they break a bone after a minor fall or impact. And osteoporosis can become disabling because it can lead to hip and spine fractures, which cause pain and immobility.
The best way to assess bone health before a break is with a special type of X-ray called a DEXA scan. MRH recently purchased a new, more sophisticated DEXA scanner to make excellent bone imaging convenient for the Craig-area community.
DEXA stands for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry. It's a quick, painless x-ray that measures the density of your bones. The denser your bones, the stronger they are. The less dense your bones, the more likely they are to break or begin to crumble as you age.
The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends that women over age 65 receive regular DEXA scans. In addition, younger women and older men with risk factors such as a family history of osteoporosis, a history of broken bones after age 50, smoking, physical inactivity, heavy alcohol use, early hysterectomy, diabetes, certain medication use (steroids, proton pump inhibitors, epilepsy drugs) and low body-mass indexes are also good candidates for DEXA scanning.
'An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,' Mucha said. 'DEXA scans are essential in making sure we can provide the best preventive care for our Craig community members.'
If your DEXA scan reveals you have worsening osteopenia or osteoporosis, Mucha will help you develop a plan to improve your bone health or stop it from worsening further.
Regular exercise and a healthy diet are good places to start. The more you use your bones to move and bear weight, the stronger they become. And diets high in calcium and vitamin D give your bones the nutrients they need to build new bone.
Often prescription medications are recommended to treat osteoporosis as well. There are medications that help slow bone loss, and there are medications that help rebuild bone. Osteoporosis can be reversed over time.
'My treatment plans range from supplements and exercises to prescribed medications,' Mucha said. 'I have routine follow-ups with patients who are on medications prescribed for osteoporosis treatment. I want my patients to be an active part of their care, and I make sure that I ‘meet them where they are at' when choosing a treatment plan with them.'
To make an appointment with Mucha, please call 970-826-2400.
Bridget Mucha, Family Nurse Practitioner, orthopedics and bone health specialist. Memorial Regional Health/Courtesy photo OLYMPUS DIGITAL CAMERA

title: Faith: God is the perfect father
author: Len Browning
description: The concept of God as our father is largely foreign to the Jew, especially in Old Testament times. References, or more commonly, inferences to God as our father in the Old Testament are infrequent,…
content:
The concept of God as our father is largely foreign to the Jew, especially in Old Testament times.
References, or more commonly, inferences to God as our father in the Old Testament are infrequent, exceptional and communal … not personal. Consider, for example:
You are the sons of the Lord your God … For you are a people holy to the Lord your God, and the Lord has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth (Deuteronomy 14:1–2).
As a father shows compassion to his children, so the Lord shows compassion to those who fear him (Psalm 103:13).
Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? For as often as I speak against him, I do remember him still. Therefore my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him, declares the Lord (Jeremiah 31:20).
So foreign a concept to the Jews, when Jesus would call God 'Our Father' or especially 'HIS' Father, they would cry out against him and even pick up stones to stone him.
That was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God (John 5:18).
For the Christian, God as our father can often be taken for granted. As commentator Gerald Bray posits:
Christians today take it for granted that God is our Father, but few people stop to think what this name really means. We know that Jesus taught his disciples to pray 'Our Father' and that the Aramaic word Abba ('Father') is one of the few that Jesus used and that it has remained untranslated in our New Testament. Nowadays, hardly anybody finds this strange and many people are surprised to discover that the Jews of Jesus' day, and even his own disciples, were puzzled by his teaching. This is because the deeper meaning and the wider implications of the term 'Father' are largely unknown today. So widespread and generally accepted has the name become that we no longer question it, and so we often fail to realize how important it is for our understanding of God.
A common misconception is that everyone is a child of God. While God is the father of all as the 'Creator of the universe,' God as Father in terms of redemption is reserved for those who have received Jesus Christ; they are the true 'children of God.'
He (Jesus) came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God, who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:11-13).
Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying 'Abba, Father!' So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God (Galatians 4:6-7).
Hopefully, you took time to celebrate your earthly father on Sunday, living or not, we have the great privilege and opportunity to honor our fathers, which is a lifelong admonition.
For some, earthly fathers were not good and maybe even abusive, for those I pray for healing and restoration.
For everyone, I pray that you would pursue the perfect father, our God in heaven, through a relationship with Jesus Christ, His Son, our Savior.

title: Officials begin investigation into Steamboat plane crash that killed two people as coroner releases names of deceased
author: John F. Russell
description: Routt County Coroner Mitch Locke released the names of the two people killed June 17 after the twin-engine plane they were flying in crashed into the West Acres neighborhood. Dan Dunn, 67, and Jessica…
content:
The area in West Acres Mobile home park was closed off by police tape on Tuesday, June 18, 2024. Two homes and some sheds were destroyed Monday afternoon after an airplane crashed in the mobile home park.
John F. Russell/Steamboat Pilot & Today
Routt County Coroner Mitch Locke released the names of the two people killed June 17 after the twin-engine plane they were flying in crashed into the West Acres neighborhood.
Dan Dunn, 67, and Jessica Pauline Melton, 42, took off from the Vance Brand Municipal Airport in Longmont at 3:17 p.m., according to FlightAware.
The plane was scheduled to fly to the Ogden-Hinckley Airport four miles southwest of Ogden, Utah. The flight was was diverted to the Bob Adams Field in Steamboat Springs roughly 40 minutes after takeoff due to apparent engine trouble.
Flight data shows the plane circled Bob Adams Field for roughly 25 minutes before the aircraft crashed into the neighborhood , killing both people on board.
The state's corporate database shows Berthoud-based High Country Aero as the registered owner of the twin-engine Cessna 421, and Dunn is listed as the company's registered agent. Both Dunn and Melton were from the Front Range.
'Our hearts go out to the families and friends of Dan and Jessica,' Steamboat Springs Police Commander Rich Brown said in a statement. 'This could have been a much larger event and I want to thank all the first responders, crisis support, interpretive services and relief personnel who responded to the West Acres neighborhood.'
Mike Lane, communications manager for the city of Steamboat Springs, said officials from the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board have arrived in Steamboat Springs to begin the investigation into the crash.
They could be seen at the crash site on Tuesday examining the wreckage as a handful of neighbors watched and recalled Monday's events.
'The FAA and NTSB are on site working with police detective Sgt. Sam Silva in conducting the investigation,' Lane said. 'That immediate crash site remains closed as they will probably still be there through (Wednesday) or the next day. All residents have returned (to their homes) except for the two homes that were destroyed in the crash.'
One of the homes was unoccupied, and Lane said he believes that it was being remodeled. He said the couple living in the other home was not in the residence at the time of the crash, and he believes they are staying with relatives in town. Police tape surrounds a home in the West Acres Mobile Home Park that was destroyed in a plane crash on Monday. The pilot and a passenger died in the crash, and the ensuing fire destroyed two homes and several nearby sheds. John F. Russell/Steamboat Pilot & Today Investigators work Tuesday at the site of a plane crash that killed two people and started a fire that destroyed two homes in the West Acres neighborhood. John F. title: Lance Scranton: Listen, learn and like each other again
author: Lance Scranton
description: I'm up in Canada for my annual trek to the Shuswaps in British Columbia to visit family. Canada is a great place to visit, I love my family, and our neighbors to the north are...
content:
I'm up in Canada for my annual trek to the Shuswaps in British Columbia to visit family. Canada is a great place to visit, I love my family, and our neighbors to the north are a friendly bunch. It says so much about people who are welcoming, especially during a time when borders have become a major talking point in most of our conversations.
So many things about cultures cross over borders, and if you aren't paying too much attention, you wouldn't notice much of a difference in the western part of North America. As I walk around neighborhoods, I see plenty of evidence that people are frustrated with their government as evidenced by the various bumper stickers (replace Biden with Trudeau and you get the picture).
Free speech is still alive in Canada, although it seems to have taken a hit lately with the passage of legislation known as C-16 that is purported to protect people from damaging speech like the type that doesn't recognize your preferred pronoun or identifier.
The other part of culture that respects no borders are the things that make our culture sustainable. Patriotism used to be taken for granted, but a Pew Research poll reports that only 38% of people think it is very important. Seems like a crushing culture destroyer if the number is accurate. Watch a hockey playoff game between the Edmonton Oilers and the Florida Panthers and you would think that everyone in Canada is absolutely rabid about being Canadian, but maybe it's more about hockey than love of country.
Faith has taken a hit as well, as only 39% find that religion is important in their lives. We all have faith in something, but organized religion seems like the place that people are staying away from, rather than flocking to for spiritual expression and comfort. Churches abound all over North America, but have continued to lose mass appeal as generations of young people have decided that their trust is lacking in organized institutions, including those of the public, private or governmental type.
It's always difficult to convince people to stay away from something because part of what it says or does is offensive, and it assumes that anyone or any institution that holds views that upset you are automatically not worth your time or attention. This erosion of vibrant discussion and polite disagreement has helped to fracture many parts of our culture on both sides of the border. As we continue to fragment into various groups, we are so much easier to manipulate and be controlled by the very same institutions we mistrust.
Relational views are also at an all-time low, as 71% of Americans are less confident in each other compared to 20 years ago. Some say that people aren't as reliable as they used to be or that we don't need each other as much as we used to. Conversely, people who are lonely are 50% more likely to die prematurely than those with healthy social relationships. We are social animals, and as we close ourselves off from other people, it is going to affect people on both sides of the border. Canadians have a reputation for being nice and Americans for being independent. Both are admirable qualities when exercised with good judgment. Shutting ourselves off from others is deadly, and we should all remember that anxiety and depression are mitigated by having friends and staying involved in life.
On July 1, Canada will celebrate their country's establishment, and on July 4, we will celebrate independence from tyranny and subjection. Both countries were founded to enjoy the advantages of self-reliance and freedom to make their own way. Having spent a good portion of my life in both countries, I'm hopeful that these poll numbers will change, or maybe even don't reflect the true nature of our two cultures that have helped shape much of the world in the last 100 years. Remember how much we truly do need each other, and regardless of our views, we need to listen, learn and start to like each other again.

title: Hayden police make felony arrest following disturbance
author: Staff Report
description: Hayden police made a felony arrest Saturday after responding to a disturbance in the 700 block of East Lincoln Avenue. Police responded to a call reporting 'individuals were fighting, and they could…
content:
Hayden police made a felony arrest Saturday after responding to a disturbance in the 700 block of East Lincoln Avenue.
Police responded to a call reporting 'individuals were fighting, and they could see at least three males involved in the altercation,' according to a press statement from the Hayden Police Department.
The statement added that two of the individuals left the scene in a vehicle prior to officers arriving and that police spoke to witnesses who reported that a suspect 'had confronted one of the (victim) parties over an allegation of property being stolen.'
Hayden police apparently located an injured party walking away from the scene and officers were alerted to a second injured party at the residence, according to the statement.
'An ambulance from the West Routt Fire Protection District was requested. While deputies from the Routt County Sheriff's Office checked the area for the suspect vehicle, officers spoke to the injured individuals,' the police statement said.
Officers reported one of the injured individuals said they were 'struck in the face with a metal object' before being chased with an 'edged weapon.'
The second injured person said he 'did not believe he was an intended target,' according to the press statement. Police said neither of the victims sustained non-life-threatening injuries and both declined medical treatment.
Officers subsequently located the suspect vehicle just before 3 p.m. and took an individual into custody.
According to the police press statement, Leiner Barquero-Cascante, 44, of Hayden was 'interviewed and booked into Routt County jail' on assault in the second degree and menacing. Both are felony charges.
Hayden police added that the incident 'appeared to be an isolated event with all parties known to one another.'
Barquero-Cascante is scheduled to appear Tuesday in Routt County Court.

title: Writers on the Range: Ditch ‘inefficiencies' give us wetlands
author: Richard Knight
description: Imagine Westerners waking up one morning only to discover that many of their most cherished wetlands have dried up, gone. This is not fiction during these times of determining the true value of water.…
content:
Since 1917, five generations have lived along the Animas Consolidated Ditch outside of Durango. Patty Zink is pictured here.
Dave Marston/Writers on the Range
Imagine Westerners waking up one morning only to discover that many of their most cherished wetlands have dried up, gone. This is not fiction during these times of determining the true value of water.
Most wetlands in the arid West owe their existence to the 'inefficiencies' of unlined irrigation canals and flood irrigation. But when well-intentioned urban folks insist that irrigation companies use water more efficiently by piping their ditches, the result may be more about loss than water 'saved' for rivers.
One of the least-known truths in the West is that many of our wetlands are the result of irrigated agriculture. For example, an irrigation company in northern Colorado irrigates about 24,000 acres, thanks to 146 miles of ditches.
The area served by the irrigation company also has approximately 1,300 acres of wetlands, and it's no accident that most of those wetlands lie below a leaking ditch. A study by Colorado State University discovered this connection using heavy isotopes to create hydrographs of groundwater wells, ditch levels and precipitation. This is a West-wide issue.
We all know that climate change has been causing hotter, drier weather, and that helps reduce the flow of the Colorado River that 40 million Westerners depend on. In the Laramie Basin of Wyoming, 67% of its wetlands are attributed to agriculture. In North Park, Colorado, close to 75% of all wetlands are byproducts of irrigated agriculture.
Decades ago, Aldo Leopold wrote, 'There are two spiritual dangers in not owning a farm. One, you think that heat comes from the furnace and two, you think that breakfast comes from the grocery store.'
May I add a third? We don't know much about the water we depend on.
Farmers and ranchers produce two 'goods,' a private good and a public good. They're compensated for the private one by producing food. Their public goods, ecosystem services, are not compensated, though they include wetlands, biodiversity and plants sequestering carbon.
But knowing that rural agriculture uses 79% of the Colorado River's water, our urban neighbors tell their rural counterparts to conserve water or, better yet, sell it to them.
Meanwhile, the environmental community would like rural agriculture to use less water so more could stay in the rivers to help fish and provide recreational opportunities.
Clearly, there are too many demands for the West's diminishing water supply. Drinking water, ag water, river health. Where do wetlands fit in?
Wetlands cover 1% of the West's land surface, yet half of our threatened and endangered species rely on them. Wetlands serve a similar function to our kidneys: They filter out impurities from human land uses, making our environment healthier.
Perhaps it's time for all of us to wise up a little. Many of these wetlands are human created; that is, they were created by farmers and ranchers and are not 'natural.' Many will disappear in the pursuit of water conservation. Must it be water conservation and efficiency at all costs?
Will we prioritize water for urban uses, including urban sprawl? Or will we support more water staying in our rivers to create a healthier environment? Will water for food production be considered a necessity? Do green lawns trump healthy rivers and wetlands?
With more informed conversations about our region, talks between rural and urban neighbors, perhaps we could pursue a triple bottom line: water for food production, water for urban uses, and, yes, water for our region's rivers, streams and wetlands
Wouldn't we all like that? Let's figure out how to make that happen.

title: Utah man dies in rafting accident in Dinosaur National Monument
author: Staff Report
description: The body of a 50-year-old man from ​Sandy, Utah has been recovered after a rafting accident during a private permitted trip on the Green River in Dinosaur National Monument. According to a news…
content:
The body of a 50-year-old man from ​Sandy, Utah was recovered Friday after a rafting accident during a private permitted trip on the Green River in Dinosaur National Monument.
Lauren Blair/file
The body of a 50-year-old man from ​Sandy, Utah has been recovered after a rafting accident during a private permitted trip on the Green River in Dinosaur National Monument.
According to a news release from the Moffat County Sheriff's Office, at or around 4 p.m. on Thursday, monument staff were notified that a boat was pinned on a rock in the rapid named Hells Half Mile. One person from the group was missing and suspected to be pinned under the raft. The group was eventually able to unpin and secure the boat, but the person, now dislodged, was unresponsive and having lost his lifejacket, drifted downriver.
River Patrol Rangers were informed and initiated travel through the Canyon of Lodore by raft to intercept the group and conduct recovery efforts. Additional support traveled by car using the Echo Park Road. At 7:45 a.m. on Friday, monument staff received information from Adrift, a commercial rafting company, that the victim's body had been found and secured by guides approximately 10 river miles downstream from the location of the accident.
With the assistance of Adrift guides, monument staff and the Vernal-based Classic Air Medical helicopter crew, the victim's body was transported to the Moffat County coroner. The rafter's name will be withheld while family members are notified.
Dinosaur National Monument expresses appreciation for Classic, Adrift, River Runners Transport, Moffat County ACTSS (Advocates, Crisis, Trauma, and Survivor Services) and monument staff who assisted in search and recovery efforts, and offers condolences to the family and river community impacted by this incident.
Hells Half Mile is a class III/IV rapid located on the Green River in the Canyon of Lodore in the Colorado portion (Moffat County) of Dinosaur National Monument. It is approximately 12 river miles downstream of the Gates of Lodore boat launch near the monument's northern boundary. Flow rates for the Canyon of Lodore section of the Green River are influenced by the water release at Flaming Gorge Dam, which averaged 4700 cubic feet per second from June 25-28.
Dinosaur National Monument consists of over 210,000 acres in both Colorado and Utah. While the monument is best known for the dinosaur quarry and the fossils preserved there, the monument also contains canyons along the Green and Yampa rivers.

title: MCSD Whiteboard: A new era in Moffat County
author: Moffat County School District
description: Last week, we bid a fond farewell to our interim superintendent Dr. Brad Meeks, who led the district onto strong ground in the midst of a tumultuous period. Meeks has set Moffat County schools on...
content:
Last week, we bid a fond farewell to our interim superintendent Dr. Brad Meeks, who led the district onto strong ground in the midst of a tumultuous period.
Meeks has set Moffat County schools on a course for success. It's up to us as a district and a community to now carry that work forward. Fortunately, we are welcoming a new leader in that effort, Mathew Neal, who officially took office on Monday, July 1.
Neal brings enormous enthusiasm and even more expertise to the important position of Moffat County School District superintendent. His experience and passion for education and community will be a major boost to the work already underway in the district. And he'll have new ideas and new directions, too. It's an exciting time.
It's a good moment to consider again just how critical this work is.
If Craig and Moffat County are going to be great, Moffat County School District must be great. The relationship between the success of the two is extraordinarily close. The district relies on the success and partnership of the community, and the community relies on the output and connective tissues of the district. Without one another, both are doomed to fail — but together, great things are possible.
MCSD is where this community is built — its future, surely, but also its present. It's in our halls, gymnasiums, theaters and classrooms that Moffat County gets together. It's where lifelong bonds are formed, both between children and between parents and guardians. It's how we keep ourselves moving.
You've really got to go searching to find Moffat County residents who are not affected by what happens in Moffat County schools. Whether it's our hundreds of employees, our nearly 2,000 students and their families, or our thousands of graduates and their employers, employees and families, education in Moffat County touches everyone. That's why it's so important to work together to achieve excellence in education.
The output touches everyone, so it only makes sense that the input would come from everyone. And it does. Whether it's funding our programming directly through property ownership, or contributing in other ways (including collaboration, partnership and assistance), the success of the district depends on what its community puts into it. We're grateful for all you do to make sure we thrive, which is how we ensure students thrive — and by extension, the community itself.
Let's step into this new era, then, with confidence, hope, and with our sleeves rolled way, way up. It's time to make Moffat County great, and we start that process in school. Join us, as you always have, and help us be the best we can be, together.

title: Health Column: Support hospice in our community at the Rubber Ducky Race on Aug. 3
author: Northwest Colorado Health
description: One of many myths about choosing hospice is that it means giving up hope. The reality is that in hospice, the hope for living each day to the fullest becomes the focus. Sally Habermehl, Director of…
content:
One of many myths about choosing hospice is that it means giving up hope. The reality is that in hospice, the hope for living each day to the fullest becomes the focus.
Sally Habermehl, Director of Home Services for Northwest Colorado Health, has been with the agency for more than 25 years. She has seen firsthand the impact that hospice has on our neighbors, and the community as a whole, in ensuring that everyone receives the compassionate care that they need at the end of life.
'Our hospice nurses often get called 'guardian angels,'' said Habermehl. 'I have had several people come up to me and say 'if I ever had to go on hospice, I would want your nurses'. We are very fortunate to have such a wonderful team of nurses, social workers, chaplains, therapists and aids in our hospice program. They all care deeply and are willing to go the extra mile to help patients as they transition through the end stage of life.'
While many believe that hospice is only for the last days of life, patients and families can receive hospice care for six months or longer. Research has shown that entering hospice earlier rather than later in the course of illness has many advantages for the patient, and loved ones.
• Better pain and symptom control. When hospice staff have more time to provide care for the patient, they can provide individualized management of pain and other symptoms, offering as much relief and comfort as possible.
• Improved quality of life. Hospice care focuses on the wellbeing of the whole patient. There is greater opportunity to focus on what matters most in life, offering more quality time with loved ones.
• Access to helpful medical supplies and equipment. A hospital bed, commode or wheelchair help caregivers cope with the increasing needs of their loved ones.
• Fewer hospital and ICU admissions. Patients admitted to hospice earlier in the course of illness are much less likely to go to a hospital or ICU in a state of crisis. They are more likely to die at home surrounded by loved ones.
• More days of life. Studies have shown that hospice patients live longer than those with a similar diagnosis who do not receive hospice care.
• Bereavement support for patient and family. Grief counseling for caregivers and patients allows them to work through emotional issues before death occurs and find peace in their final days. Support for families continues after the death of a loved one.
'Hospice is about the quality of life that exists in the process of dying,' said Jo Anne Grace, Spiritual Care and Bereavement Coordinator with Northwest Colorado Health's Hospice program. 'When we have time to establish a network of support around a patient and family, we are able to encourage final wishes and pinpoint what that person wants to accomplish before they die. Hospice allows family members a respite from 24/7 caregiving so they can re-establish a relationship with their loved one not focused on duty. They are able to relax from their role and instead focus on just being with their loved one.'
Northwest Colorado Health has provided comfort-oriented end-of-life hospice care in the Yampa Valley for nearly 30 years. As a nonprofit hospice provider, Northwest Colorado Health provides care to all residents who need it, regardless of their ability to pay. Although health insurance may cover hospice, expenses such as medications, equipment and bereavement support often exceed reimbursement. Donations and fundraising events like the Rubber Ducky Race for Hospice help cover this gap.
The Craig Rubber Ducky Race for Hospice is an opportunity for Moffat County residents to support this service in their communities. The race will take place on Aug. 3 at the Moffat County Hot Air Balloon Festival starting at 11:00 a.m. Tickets are only $10, and contestants can win cash and other prizes. Purchase tickets at NorthwestColoradoHealth.org/rubberducky .
To learn more about Northwest Colorado Health's hospice program, visit NorthwestColoradoHealth.org/hospice or call 970-871-7629.
Northwest Colorado Health is currently hiring multiple positions within the Home Services Department, including a part-time hospice chaplain and a Medical Social Worker for Home Health and Hospice. Please visit our website to learn more and apply.

title: Wearing life jackets critical to stem rising number of Colorado drownings
author: Suzie Romig
description: So far this year, Colorado Parks & Wildlife boating safety officials have recorded 26 deaths on all Colorado waterways and water bodies in only four months from March through July 2. CPW Boating Law…
content:
Free loaner life jackets are available at many large, well-visited water bodies in Colorado, including Pearl Lake State Park in northern Routt County.
Suzie Romig/Craig Press
So far this year, Colorado Parks & Wildlife boating safety officials have recorded 26 deaths on all Colorado waterways and water bodies in only four months from March through July 2.
CPW Boating Law Administrator Grant Brown said the common denominator for those drownings and fatalities, reported to or verified by the state agency, is not wearing a life vest or personal floatation device.
Brown said the data shows most of the drowning deaths involved adult males, winds, cold water, and the majority, on lakes or flat water.
'Regardless of your age or experience level, cold water can quickly create a drowning emergency,' according to CPW. 'Only boat or paddle in conditions you are comfortable and confident paddling in. Boat and raft with a buddy, and avoid floating alone, especially during high flows.'
Even when the air temperatures are warmer, many Colorado water bodies retain colder water temperatures that can cause cold water immersion shock that can trigger involuntary gasping, rapid breathing or hyperventilating, Brown said.
In Colorado, children age 12 and younger are required to wear a personal floatation device whenever they are on a vessel on the water, except when they are in an enclosed cabin or below deck. A vessel includes paddleboards, kayaks, canoes, and all types of boats and watercraft, except for single-chamber blow-up devices such as inner tubes.
In 2023, CPW tracked 32 water-related fatalities, a state record-setting 42 deaths in 2022, 22 deaths in 2021 and 34 deaths in 2020.
U.S. Coast Guard statistics show that drowning was the reported cause of death in four out of every five recreational boating fatalities in 2021, and 83 percent of those who drowned were not wearing life jackets.
