title: Neal believes relationships are the heart of education
author: John Chalstrom
description: Mathew Neal was handed the reigns of the Moffat County School District on July 1 and has embarked on an ambitious start towards his journey as the superintendent of schools. Growing up on a ranch...
content:
Mathew Neal assumed the responsibilities of superintendent of the Moffat County School District on July 1.
Moffat County School District/Courtesy photo
Mathew Neal was handed the reigns of the Moffat County School District on July 1 and has embarked on an ambitious start towards his journey as the superintendent of schools.
Growing up on a ranch in between Fort Collins and Walden, Neal saw Craig as an opportunity to return to his roots and lead a school district that embodied the values of hard work, strong community connection and a school district ready for stability.
Having been in the district for only two weeks, Neal's calendar is already full. His primary goal in his first 100 days on the job is to meet with as many community members as possible. Having already met with 27 community leaders in eight days, Neal was also conducting one-on-one conversations with the members of the board of directors.
'Listening and learning are essential,' Neal said.
And it is his hope that through dialog with stakeholders that a collaborative vision can be formulated that will advance the district.
A strong proponent of systems thinking, Neal was quick to express that 'relationships are the heart of education. I wish to create a culture based on community.'
Among the groups that Neal is planning on strong engagement with is the ministerial association, city government leaders and the business community. A pastor's breakfast is being organized to bring spiritual leaders together to help strengthen the bonds with the school district and provide support when needed.
The challenges facing the district are many and Neal is well aware of the hurdles he may be facing. Serving as the fourth superintendent in as many years, he would like to bring a sense of stability and continuity to the district and begin working on long-range goals that can be implemented with fidelity and collaboration.
With uncertainty facing the district in light of impending closures of the power plant and coal mine, Neal hopes to work with other community leaders to develop a positive vision for the future of the region that has found itself in the midst of economic and social transition. Changing demographics and enrollment patterns will force the district to make adjustments but Neal feels that this can be done in a constructive and proactive manner.
Specific initiatives that Neal feels need to be addressed in the short-term include crisis and facilities planning. Working with the board to develop mutually connected goals, Neal feels that a comprehensive facilities plan needs to be developed to address the learning needs of students and staff. Likewise, a sound safety and security plan needs to be implemented that is created in harmony with the school district's resource officers and the local law enforcement community.
Perhaps the most pressing issue facing the district that Neal hopes to address is unity. Superintendent turnover may have led to individual buildings acting as 'disconnected silos.'
Neal hopes to bring all buildings and entities in the district into one fold noting that 'Decentralization does not work. The better systems are, the better able they are able to service students.'
Quoting French author Alexandre Dumas from the novel 'The Three Musketeers,' Neal hopes that all employees of the district adhere to the mantra of 'all for one, and one for all.'
Neal comes to Moffat County with vast experience in education. Receiving his bachelor's degree from Mississippi College, Neal started his career as a business education teacher before earning his master's of business administration from Colorado State University. He earned his doctorate in education from the University of Southern California and also received a certificate of superintendent leadership from Harvard University.
His educational administrative journey has seen him serve as the Executive Director of the Brighton/Durango School Districts, the Director of Strategy and Innovation for the Denver Public Schools, Superintendent of the Sweetwater County School District in Rock Springs, Wyoming, Superintendent of the International Baccalaurate American Schools Middle East in Kuwait and as the President of MRJB Educational Consulting in Colorado.
Neal's family is settling in to the community after purchasing a home in Craig. His wife will be teaching in neighboring Steamboat Springs will his children will be attending middle and high school in Moffat County. In his free time, Neal enjoys all that Colorado has to offer including mountain biking, skiing and spending time with family.
The Moffat County School Board extended Neal a three-year contract upon his acceptance of the position and will be compensated $175,000 for his first year of employment. While an increase from his predecessor, it is typical for incoming superintendents to earn more than an outgoing school leader. Neighboring district Steamboat Springs, a district of comparable size, payed their superintendent $210,000 during the 2023-24 school year.

title: Cataract surgery with light adjustable lenses can help avoid distance glasses
author: Suzie Romig
description: Longtime Steamboat Springs ophthalmologist Dr. Mark Helm eagerly watched research studies and waited 20 years for the release of a high-tech version of cataract surgery lenses so that more patients…
content:
Ophthalmologist Dr. Mark Helm, shown last week in his Steamboat Springs clinic, eagerly watched and waited for 20 years to be able to perform cataract surgery with a Light Adjustable Lens.
Helm Eye Center/Courtesy photo
Longtime Steamboat Springs ophthalmologist Dr. Mark Helm eagerly watched research studies and waited 20 years for the release of a high-tech version of cataract surgery lenses so that more patients could avoid using distance glasses after the common eye surgery.
Even after performing more than 5,000 cataract surgeries since 1992, Helm is excited to talk about the Light Adjustable Lens technology, which still strikes him as 'pretty Star Trek.'
'I'm absolutely still impressed with whole process,' Helm said. 'Patients are getting a new component in the eye that is just as high-tech as it can be.'
Since July 2021, Helm has performed 125 of the cataract surgeries using the new lens that can be fine-tuned for patients' vision weeks after the surgery by using a Light Delivery Device with targeted ultraviolet light.
Although the advanced lenses inserted into the eye during cataract removal procedures are not covered by insurance and cost $4,000 more per eye, it can help 98% of cataract surgery patients avoid the use of glasses for distance vision, according to Helm.
Steamboat Springs resident Pam Brenner, 70, is one of those folks happy to receive the Light Adjustable Lens.
'When it came up on me, the cataract was dramatic,' Brenner said. 'I saw a lot of glare. I just wasn't able to see the computer screen that well, and I am still working full time. My vision is very important to me. I wanted to be able to see without using glasses.' RxSight, based in California, has developed a Light Adjustable Lens for cataract surgery, shown here with a reusable injector system. RxSight/Courtesy photo
After Brenner's cataract surgery in her right eye in April, Helm adjusted the lens to her preferred vision level, and she does not need to use glasses now.
'People have the choice to get three different adjustments to get their vision to where they want it to be that works best for them,' said Brenner, who is an avid golfer.
Steamboat resident Tee Murray, 78, a ski instructor for 52 years, also is pleased with his high-tech cataract surgery results — especially to eliminate glare he experienced previously when driving at night. He said the procedure has been a 'game changer' to help his vision when skiing, fishing and biking.
Following day surgery at UCHealth Yampa Valley Medical Center to insert the lens, patients work with the doctor at the Helm Eye Center ophthalmology office in Steamboat to receive the specialized light treatments. Then, the adjustable lens is locked into a set, permanent focus.
'The special type of UV light does not cause any damage to any part of the eye,' Helm explained of the high-tech Light Delivery Device.
According to lens manufacturer RxSight, based in California, 'in a study of 600 subjects, those who received the Light Adjustable Lens followed by adjustment were twice as likely to achieve 20/20 vision at six months without glasses as those who receive a standard/fixed mono-focal intraocular lens.'
Cataract surgery is the most common surgery performed on an outpatient basis in the U.S. at approximately 3.5 million surgeries each year, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. The eye surgeon cuts or lasers a tiny incision in the cornea, and the cataract clouding the natural lens is broken up with ultrasonic energy, a process called phacoemulsification. The cataract is suctioned out with a tiny medical wet vacuum instrument, and then a clear, synthetic lens is inserted to replace the natural lens.
About 50% of Americans will develop cataracts by age 75, a percentage that is projected to increase as life expectancies continue to rise. Cataracts form when the proteins and fibers in an eye's natural lens begin to break down, causing hazy or cloudy vision, according to RxSight. Until the customizable Light Adjustable Lens, eye doctors had to rely on the accuracy of pre-surgery measurements to determine a patient's prescription power.
Helm said most of his cataract patients start to develop the lens cloudiness in their 50s, but cannot perceive it yet. The cataracts usually progress slowly, and the decision to have cataract surgery is up to the patients and their level of visual impairment. Ophthalmologist Dr. Mark Helm, at the machine in the background, has performed more than 5,000 cataract surgeries since 1992, largely in Steamboat Springs (including shown here in 2017). Helm Eye Center/Courtesy photo
Helm Eye Center was the second practice in Colorado to incorporate the RxSight technology that is now used in 16 practices in Colorado and 732 practices across the nation, according to Jeannette Fraterelli with RxSight. Ophthalmologist Dr. Nathan Hamburger at Helm Eye Center also performs the new procedure and adjustments.
Due to the added expense, Helm said only about 10-15% of patients so far have chosen the Light Adjustable Lens. However, Helm finds that 98% of his adjustable lens patients do not have to wear glasses for distance, compared to 75-80% who do with a traditional lens implant.
Despite the cost factor, Helm said a 'vast majority' of cataract patients are 'good candidates' for the adjustable lenses.

title: MCSD Whiteboard: A great time to be grateful
author: Moffat County School District
description: This past weekend, we celebrated our nation's independence. What a great moment that is every year to remember what makes this country special — as well as what makes Moffat County special. The United…
content:
This past weekend, we celebrated our nation's independence. What a great moment that is every year to remember what makes this country special — as well as what makes Moffat County special.
The United States isn't the only country founded on ideals of liberty and opportunity, but it's one of the best success stories among those that were. There are many reasons why.
We were blessed with a brilliant, inspired system of government, and generation after generation have held sacred what made it work, and iterated carefully to improve upon what didn't.
We were blessed with a vast, dynamic, diverse land full of abundant natural resources and space.
We've been blessed with people from all parts of the world who, in the very act of choosing to leave their ancestral homes and venture to a new place with the intention of trying to set out to make the best of a great opportunity, have endowed each generation with a can-do spirit, a belief in self and in community, and a creative drive.
Does that sound familiar to you? It kind of sounds like Moffat County.
Moffat County is a place where people come on purpose. You don't end up in Craig, or in Maybell, or in Lay, or in Brown's Park, or wherever else by accident. People come here — whether it's the old homesteaders or our most recent newcomers — because they want to be here. Here, specifically. And that, combined with our abundant resources, our adherence to wise governance and the inherent can-do spirit, belief in self and community and creative drive, is what makes Moffat County great.
Much like the nation, we're facing challenges. And much like the U.S., we've got to come together to face them. That's what Moffat County School District feels is its mission. We say it like this: To educate and inspire students to thrive in an environment of change. If you believe in the future of the United States, you've got to invest in building it, shaping it, protecting it and developing it. If you believe in the future of Moffat County, you've got to invest in education.
That's what we're here for, and we need your help. This summer, let's cheer on our teachers, our staff, and our administrators. Let's cheer on our students most of all. Because come fall, we've got serious work to do in these school buildings. The future of the county depends on it.
We're grateful, Moffat County. Grateful for you. Grateful for this place. Grateful for this country. We honor those who dedicate their lives to protecting it, serving it, building it and developing it. We honor those who have come before, and those who are here now. Thank you to you all.

title: Group that manages Moto Complex receives $10,000 grant
author: Staff Report
description: Northwest Colorado Trails Corp has received a Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative grant of $10,000 for the repair and maintenance of Megawatt Moto Complex. The grant was awarded as part of an ongoing…
content:
Northwest Colorado Trails Corp has received a Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative grant of $10,000 for the repair and maintenance of Megawatt Moto Complex.
The grant was awarded as part of an ongoing effort to encourage safe, responsible riding and sustainable, open riding areas in Craig.
Northwest Colorado Trails Corp is a nonprofit that works in cooperation with trail clubs, crews and organizations in support of the trail systems in Northwest Colorado. Northwest Colorado Trails currently manage Megawatt Moto Complex on Moffat Country Road 107 in Craig.
According to the organization, NWCTC works to maintain an association of persons interested in trail maintenance, preservation and expansion; to assist in the development, promotion, and completion of trail services, facilities and programs; acts as a liaison between the community and trail clubs, crews and organizations; and works to increase public awareness and stimulate the use and preservation of the trail systems in Northwest Colorado.
Megawatt Moto Complex is an 182 parcel of county land that has had a motocross track in place since the 1980s. In addition to the MX track, there is a youth track, a beginner's circle, enduro skills obstacle training area, turn track training area and three enduro trails.
For more information about Yamaha's Outdoor Access Initiative, YamahaOAI.com

title: Kum and Go being rebranded as Maverik this week
description: An inconvenience may be experienced in Craig, Hayden and Steamboat Springs the next two weeks as four Kum and Go stores will be closed for the purpose of 're-branding.' Kum and Go, a subsidiary of...
content:
Five Kum and Go convenience stores in Craig, Hayden and Steamboat Springs will be closed over the next two weeks for the purpose of "re-branding." The stores will reopen under the name "Maverik."
Sasha Nelson/Craig Press
An inconvenience may be experienced in Craig, Hayden and Steamboat Springs the next two weeks as four Kum and Go stores will be closed for the purpose of 're-branding.'
Kum and Go, a subsidiary of the Des Moines, Iowa-based Krause Group, was sold to Maverik, a Salt Lake City-based convenience store chain in August 2023. Maverik plans to rebrand all of its stores by the end of 2025.
According to the Maverik website, the Hayden Kum and Go closed Monday and will reopen July 23.
In Craig, closures will be somewhat staggered. The 700 Victory Way store will close July 16 and reopen July 23. At its 895 Yampa Ave. location, the store will close July 17 and reopen on July 23. The 1302 W. Victory Way location will close July 21 and open for business July 30.
Steamboat Springs is host to two Kum and Go stores. The Angler's Bay location was rebranded in June while the 2032 Curve Plaza store will close July 22-30.
Patrons who are members of the Kum and Go Rewards program are advised to use accumulated points prior to the store closures as they will not roll over to the Maverik stores.

title: Moffat County FBLA students hone business prowess at national event
author: Andy Bockelman
description: Heading into the business world of tomorrow will involve one lesson after another, and the members of Moffat County High School's FBLA chapter already have a considerable leg up. Moffat County was…
content:
From left, Moffat County students Travis LeFevre, Wyatt Tucker, Jonah Jenison, Caroline Schenck, Hannah Kilpatrick, Aliza Johnson and Carson Laehr gather during the 2024 FBLA National Leadership Conference in Orlando, Florida.
Courtesy Photo
Heading into the business world of tomorrow will involve one lesson after another, and the members of Moffat County High School's FBLA chapter already have a considerable leg up.
Moffat County was well-represented during the Future Business Leaders of America National Leadership Conference in late June and early July in Orlando, Florida, with six of the Bulldogs competing in business-related topics.
Though none of the MCHS students went on to the final rounds, the sheer number of participants at this level was impressive, MCHS teacher Krista Schenck said.
Initially, junior Hannah Kilpatrick was the lone MoCo student in the program to move on from the state event in April, placing fourth in graphic design, with the top six qualifiers going to nationals. Kilpatrick also went to DECA nationals earlier this year.
However, juniors Aliza Johnson and Travis LeFevre each learned that because other higher-ranked competitors were unable to make the trip, they would be able to head to Orlando in the FBLA categories of business management and marketing, respectively.
Just before the registration deadline, the trio of Carson Laehr, Jonah Jenison and Wyatt Tucker also secured a spot in the broadcast journalism event.
'I would say that the pressure is less than it was for the state competition,' Laehr said. 'Nationals is the biggest event, but we made it as far as we could.'
Recent graduate Caroline Schenck also went to FBLA nationals with the group as an adviser.
Johnson said the recent competition was tough but beneficial as a more intense challenge in the form of a written test.
'My test was all about business management styles, accounting and problem-solving in the workplace,' she said.
As a vice president of FBLA in the past school year, Johnson is setting her sights on being DECA president in the fall.
'I definitely learned to take a bit more initiative when it comes to group settings,' she said. 'I can use my learned skills to be a good leader and take charge when it comes to incoming members and help them feel welcome in the team.'
Johnson said she plans to get a business degree in college, likely at University of Northern Colorado, and FBLA has been crucial for her building toward that goal.
'I'm usually given a problem such as helicoptering management under me or employees not following through on tasks, or something like that. Then I have to come up with ideas to advise the company to fix that,' she said. 'I already felt fairly confident in my public speaking skills, but I didn't exactly know how to portray myself in the right way for starting a presentation. That's really helped me in finding the right way to present yourself.'
LeFevre, who is also going into his senior year, noted that the first year of getting involved in FBLA events after already being part of the DECA team helped him think differently.
'FBLA had a lot larger range of events, and it's not so focused on certain aspects like DECA is,' he said. 'DECA is almost all role-play, not so much prepared presentation events like we do for FBLA The prep time is different, so it affects the quality of your presentation.'
In his case, he learned a lot of new things from the FBLA marketing.
'You can use it for speaking skills, it gives you confidence, helps you later in life be able to come up with a plan quickly,' LeFevre said. '(FBLA and DECA) are both fun, so I couldn't say if one is better — they're just different.'
Laehr, who graduated from MCHS in May, said that while broadcast journalism is not something he plans to pursue as a job — he'll attend Colorado School of Mines and major in mechanical engineering with a focus on aerospace engineering — the unique experience he got was invaluable.
'I think that DECA and FBLA have both helped prepare for a career and adult life in a lot of ways, in being able to get everyone to think critically in a short amount of time to solve a problem and in being able to meet so many like-minded people,' he said. 'One of the things I'll always remember is the amount of little conversations I've had with strangers who I would have never met otherwise. It has definitely been a great experience to meet so many people. When I joined I wasn't quite sure what to expect. I joined because I had some friends who were in the clubs, but it was a lot more fun than I originally anticipated it being.' More Like This, Tap A Topic education

title: Moffat County recent grad receives scholarship through Credit Union of Colorado Foundation
author: Staff Report
description: Moffat County High School 2024 graduate Megan Neton will receive a $5,000 scholarship from Credit Union of Colorado Foundation. Credit Union of Colorado Foundation announced earlier this month the 10…
content:
Megan Neton delivers the commencement address during the graduation ceremony for Moffat County High School on Saturday, May 25, 2024. Neton is among 10 students in Colorado who have been awarded a scholarship from the Credit Union of Colorado Foundation.

'This year's recipients are not only accomplished academically but also dedicated volunteers who serve their schools and communities. The future is bright with these students who will no doubt make lasting impacts in both their careers and communities.' More Like This, Tap A Topic education

title: Colorado's July wolf activity map includes update on hazing rumors, wolf pups
author: Elliott Wenzler
description: Colorado's collared wolves largely remained in Routt, Grand, Summit and Jackson counties and somewhat withdrew from some areas like Eagle County over the past month, according to a map released by…
content:
Monthly Collared Wolf Activity Area Map - July, 2024
Monthly Collared Wolf Activity Area Map – July, 2024
Colorado's collared wolves largely remained in Routt, Grand, Summit and Jackson counties and somewhat withdrew from some areas like Eagle County over the past month, according to a map released by Colorado Parks and Wildlife Wednesday.
The map, posted on the agency's website , uses Colorado watershed boundaries to indicate where wolves have been detected and reflects movements from June 25 through July 23. It is updated on the fourth Wednesday of every month. State officials have released the maps monthly since January after reintroducing 10 wolves in Grand and Summit counties in December.
In its update Wednesday, Parks and Wildlife also addressed rumors on social media that claim the agency's tracking planes are intentionally flying low to drive the wolves away from the Wyoming border. The agency said this is untrue while clarifying its staff uses the planes only to track the wolves.
Wildlife officials are also searching for evidence of wolf pups after confirming one born in Grand County earlier this year. So far they haven't seen evidence of any others.
The wolves that were released in December, which were transported to the state from Oregon, have tracking collars that record their position once every four hours. Two of those collars are no longer functioning, but those wolves are traveling with other collared wolves, according to Parks and Wildlife. One of those wolves was killed by a mountain lion in April in Larimer County.
The map only shows what watershed boundaries wolves have entered, not exact locations. Even though the map includes watersheds that cross below I-70 , the wolves haven't traveled below the interstate, according to Parks and Wildlife.
Since the start of reintroduction, there have been 13 confirmed cases of wolves attacking livestock in the state, also known as depredation. Only one of the depredation cases has resulted in a payout from the state so far.

title: Smartphone app reports 40-acre wildfire on Duffy Mountain in Moffat County
author: Eli Pace
description: A wildfire was reported at 4 p.m. Tuesday southwest of Craig in the Duffy Mountain area, according to the smartphone app Watch Duty. Based on updates posted by Watch Duty, the blaze named the Duffy...
content:
A wildfire was reported at 4 p.m. Tuesday southwest of Craig in the Duffy Mountain area, according to the smartphone app Watch Duty.
Based on updates posted by Watch Duty , the blaze named the Duffy Fire had grown to 30 acres by 5:27 p.m. and 40 acres by 6:56 p.m.
The location of the fire appears to be in or close to the Little Yampa Canyon special recreation management area that's managed by the Bureau of Land Management.
According to the BLM, the Duffy Mountain Area is a popular place for hunting, fishing and off-highway vehicles.
Watch Duty is a nonprofit wildfire alerting, mapping and tracking service. In tax filings, the nonprofit describes itself as 'a nonpartisan and nongovernment organization focused on disseminating public safety information in realtime from verified sources.'
The Alexander Mountain Fire and Stone Canyon Fire currently burning on the Front Range are both also listed in the app.
As of 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, the Inciweb.wildfire.gov/ did not have any information or indication for the Duffy Fire in Moffat County or the Stone Canyon Fire, which started Tuesday outside of Lyons.
Moffat County has spent the last two days under a red flag warning indicating favorable weather conditions for wildfires.
This developing story will be updated when more information becomes available. The nonprofit Watch Duty is reporting that a wildfire flared up Tuesday, July 30, 2024, southwest of Craig. Watch Duty

title: Residents asked to donate blood during national shortage
author: Staff Report
description: The extreme heat affecting much of the country and summer vacation season are contributing to low blood donor turnout during 'trauma season' when injuries from outdoor activities can increase,…
content:
A number of factors are contributing to low blood donor turnout and a national blood shortage.
Courtesy Photo
The extreme heat affecting much of the country and summer vacation season are contributing to low blood donor turnout during 'trauma season' when injuries from outdoor activities can increase, according to Vitalant, a nonprofit that hosts blood drives in the Yampa Valley.
Vitalant Communications Manager Brooke Way said blood donations during the Fourth of July holiday week plummeted about 30% from weekly averages, resulting in about 760 units uncollected in Colorado.
That shortfall is on top of about 8,000 fewer donations than needed nationwide in June.
'Additionally, the number of people donating with Vitalant has not rebounded from a 20% drop since 2019,' Way said. 'Among the causes, workplace blood drives have been slow to come back since the pandemic with people working remotely, and personal routines have shifted.'
Blood donors are critical to overcoming the shortage, so Vitalant is offering a $10 gift card for donors and a chance to win a $10,000 grocery giveaway.
'Vitalant urges all eligible blood donors to make an appointment to give now for the coming days and weeks to boost the blood supply for patients in need,' Way noted.
That includes an emergency shortage of type O blood, which is the most transfused blood type. O-negative blood can be used to help any patient, and O-positive can help any patient with A-positive, B-positive, AB-positive or O-positive blood. Donors of all other blood types and platelet donations also are urgently needed, Way said.
Upcoming blood drives in Steamboat Springs are set for 12:30-6 p.m. Aug. 7 at the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, 1155 Central Park Drive, and 9 a.m.-1 p.m. Aug. 8 at Colorado Mountain College auditorium, 1275 Crawford Ave.
Blood drives in Craig are planned for 9 a.m.-1 p.m. Sept. 11 at the Pavilion Building at Moffat County Fairgrounds, 640 E. Victory Way, as well as 12:30-6 p.m. Nov. 12 at the same location.
Donors can sign up at Donors.Vitalant.org .
Blood donors help ensure patients, such as northern Routt County resident Chelsea Romig, maintain the energy needed to stay active, according to Way. An avid hiker, Romig went to the doctor when she experienced fatigue and difficulty breathing.
Through several months, she received eight units of blood and was diagnosed with blood-related diseases, including hemolytic anemia, which destroys red blood cells in the body faster than the body can produce. Blood transfusions are a continued part of her treatment.
'Blood has given me my life back,' Romig said. 'It's something I didn't necessarily appreciate until now. I couldn't hike last year and thought I might never be able to do it again.'
Learn more at Vitalant.org or call 877-25-VITAL.

title: Mathew Neal: A big thank you to spiritual leaders who impact our kids
author: Mathew Neal
description: Whether you consider yourself a coach or mentor, whether you volunteer your time or get paid as a pastor, those of us within the Moffat County School system recognize that it takes a giant team...
content:
Whether you consider yourself a coach or mentor, whether you volunteer your time or get paid as a pastor, those of us within the Moffat County School system recognize that it takes a giant team to help our kids find their paths to success.
We know the numbers, which tell us that a student who has positive leaders or mentors in their life encouraging them and helping them set goals to achieve are notably more successful than a student without such factors.
As we enter the new 2024-25 school year in Moffat County, it's important to recognize that the first few weeks for students can be a challenge, especially if friend groups change or as students move up into middle or high school. During these times of growth and change, we see internally how our coaches and staff step up into the role of mentor for many of our students to help them navigate all the newness that comes with this season.
It takes a great deal of energy and patience from our teacher team to remain focused on improving student academic skills in the classroom while also helping students adapt to new classes or new social environments. We have amazing staff who should be really proud of their great work.
Over the next few weeks, we will be also thanking a different set of leaders in our community for standing strong with our students (and families) when going back to school after an amazing summer break. Many of our pastors and spiritual leaders (as well as Boys and Girls clubs, Scouts, 4-H clubs and others) provide guidance and fun, meaningful activities to our youth as the summer rolls into the new school year. I cannot minimize the positive contribution that these leaders have on our youth.
Spiritual leaders often fill that gap between parents and kids, and, as our students grow up, these leaders add tremendously to the skills that a young person has in their arsenal to adapt into the next stages of life. Spiritual leaders provide another 'trusted adult' voice, and sometimes students listen to the exact same advice from their pastor that they might not have listened to from their parents, who, to them, seemed 'out of touch.'
The reality is that many of our kids simply need another voice in their life, almost like an echo of their parents to remind them of the best path to follow when hard decisions come. For all of these and many other reasons, we at the school district pause and celebrate spiritual leader contributions to our students.
We are entering an amazing new 2024-2025 school year and we know that, as students arrive in our classrooms and navigate each of their own personal journeys in the days ahead, they are much better-suited for success because these leaders and others serving community youth have supported them along the way. Keep up the great work leaders. From inside the school classroom to all those supporting outside the schools, we are tremendously grateful for all you've provided to our students this summer.
We're off to a better MCSD school start because of all your summer support to our great students.
Thank you for all you do. See you at school! Mathew Neal Moffat County School District/Courtesy photo

title: YVEA deenergizing Maybell substation due to wildfire
author: Staff Report
description: Due to a wildfire in the area, Yampa Valley Electric Association is deenergizing its Maybell Substation. This outage impacts Maybell, Elk Springs, Sunbeam, Lookout Mountain and surrounding areas. This…
content:
Due to a wildfire in the area, Yampa Valley Electric Association is deenergizing its Maybell Substation.
This outage impacts Maybell, Elk Springs, Sunbeam, Lookout Mountain and surrounding areas.
This outage impacts roughly 300 members. YVEA is deenergizing these lines for the safety of fire crews and YVEA members. Members who are without power should plan for an extended outage, and YVEA will be providing updates on its website and Facebook as information comes from emergency officials and crews. title: The Bock's Office: ‘Deadpool' trilogy ends an era with a bang — in a good way
author: Andy Bockelman
description: The rules of comic book movies seem to change every year, if not every day, so it only makes logical sense that the biggest rule-breaker of them all has a story that keeps pushing boundaries...
content:
The title heroes have mixed reactions to their latest predicament in "Deadpool & Wolverine." The movie is about Deadpool searching the multiverse for the help of Wolverine to save the world as they know it.
Courtesy Photo
The rules of comic book movies seem to change every year, if not every day, so it only makes logical sense that the biggest rule-breaker of them all has a story that keeps pushing boundaries in the most unexpected ways.
But, the title characters of 'Deadpool & Wolverine' just keep finding ways to surprise us all, don't they, bub?
Wade Wilson (Ryan Reynolds) is finding out the hard way that experimenting with alternate timelines can have consequences.
Boring consequences.
Stuck as a car salesman rather than suiting up as the antihero Deadpool, life is more predictable and easy, but it's certainly not better.
Fortunately, the Merc with a Mouth always manages to attract weird, dangerous situations sooner or later, and being hauled in by the Time Variance Authority is just the diversion he needs after several years of horrible normalcy.
The only catch? All of humanity depends on it.
Hopping his way across alternate versions of Earth, DP just needs to find the one person with whom he's always wanted to team up: the Wolverine (Hugh Jackman).
Any day that starts with you ritualistically stapling a toupee to your head is a life where you've lost a little too much of your spontaneity, and Reynolds' latest turn as the red and black-suited wiseguy is one that takes more time getting back into character.
All part of the process, however, given the in-media-res opening we're shown right away as Deadpool plunders the ending of another movie, namely the one that gave the most credibility to the X-Universe. Say what you will about his unwillingness to hold anything sacred, but the man knows how to use a corpse's adamantium-laced skeleton to his advantage in a fight.
But that ties neatly into his search for a certain partner, and Jackman also gives us a slightly different version of the superhero he's been playing for nearly a quarter-century. If you loved him as a noble sacrificer in 'Logan,' get ready to feel annoyed with him as a morose and self-pitying Wolverine, one who's quicker to take to the booze and cigars — Wouldn't you with that healing factor? — because he's got nothing and no one left.
As bad as that sounds, there are worse things than being inconsequential. Like being designated an 'anchor being,' the most important person in a given timeline, whose absence causes the powers that be — in the form of a stuffy time bureaucrat named Paradox (Matthew Macfadyen) — feel it's easier to just erase it all once you die.
I guess what they're trying to say is, 'Thank you for doing at least one more movie, Hugh, but how does it feel to share the spotlight? Feels good, right, buddy? Maybe you can un-snikt those claws?'
The joyful sensation of Wolvie in his proper yellow and blue costume — because some of us never got over those generic black, 'Matrix'-inspired uniforms from 2000's 'X-Men' — is only part of the fan service here, with plenty of doozies that you've no doubt been wondering about over the years.
Like, what if Wolverine were the actual size he is in the comics?
Or what if somebody else briefly put on those iconic sideburns?
Or how long can two guys who are borderline immortal stab each other before they get all tuckered out?
Or what car does Deadpool find absolutely unacceptable for action?
Take that, Honda Odyssey!
With his meta-commentary and preferences for non-linear storytelling, DP is the perfect character to handle this transitional stage in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, that delicate act of inserting the X-Men into it correctly. With Reynolds contributing to a writing team that also includes director Shawn Levy, you know that very few suggestions were left unattempted in a movie that's clearly itching to throw caution and structure to the collective winds.
We've been training for this moment with the soft introduction in 'Ms. Marvel,' we got a better idea of the TVA and the multiverse from 'Loki,' and this year has also seen the glorious and timely cartoon reboot of 'X-Men '97.'
But even if you aren't staying glued to everything in the MCU that airs on Disney+, fret not, fellow nitpicker! This installment features deep cuts you didn't even realize you were missing!
Besides reminding us that yes, there were two passable 'Fantastic 4' films made in what seems like a lifetime ago, this purposely byzantine story gives us recompense for the forgotten legends of the Marvel banner, the characters with missed potential, and the ideas that didn't get past pre-production.
Not to mention a cavalcade of variations on the MCU's newest weirdo — trust me, the one you're accustomed to is by no means the greatest oddball. But if you aren't showing Dogpool the proper respect, watch your back.
It's chaotic, it's filthy, it's heartwarming, it's genuinely frustrating at times, but 'Deadpool & Wolverine' is the amalgamation of odds and ends that makes this franchise work, especially allowing for its expansion.
We're in Phase Five now, people, and there's still plenty more the House of Mouse has planned.
Now that we're officially a big happy family — at least according to the retcon — it's OK to look back on the old X-films fondly while also anticipating what still is yet to come with this new arrangement.
This could have been given the sequel designation of 3.5 for either of the two leads, because even though he's had fewer starring ventures, it's much more Reynolds' film than Jackman's.
If Logan is a little more cuddly and casual as a result of having his funny bone tickled by the foul-mouthed ninja, that's how it should be, peanut. The guy who can make you laugh from beginning to end gets to be the hero this time.

title: New downtown Craig salon Rare to host grand opening
author: Andy Bockelman
description: With a name that implies uniqueness, a new salon in downtown Craig plans to have every customer who enters its doors feeling a little more special by the time they leave. Rare Beauty Co. will...
content:
Avery Atkin and Karmen Jeannerett pose with their branded trucker hats outside Rare Beauty Co. The new downtown salon at 458 Yampa Ave. will host its grand opening Saturday, Aug. 17, 2024.
Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
With a name that implies uniqueness, a new salon in downtown Craig plans to have every customer who enters its doors feeling a little more special by the time they leave.
Rare Beauty Co. will host its grand opening from 1-3 p.m. Saturday at 458 Yampa Ave. The grand opening will include raffles, custom-made trucker hats, Italian cream soda bar and more.
Though this will be their grand opening, owners Avery Atkin and Karmen Jeannerett have been open for business since the start of July.
Atkin graduated from Moffat County High School this spring, spending the majority of her senior year getting on-the-job training at Colorado Northwestern Community College's cosmetology program.
Atkin said she had always leaned toward a career in the beauty industry but was increasingly sure it was what she wanted to do the more she learned the ins and outs of the business. Karmen Jeannerett, left, and Avery Atkin display their selfie wall at Rare Beauty Co. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
'I just like making people feel more confident and feel better about themselves in general,' she said.
Besides styling services, she will be providing salon specialties such as facials and waxing. Atkin joked that the latter makes hair care a double threat.
'If you want it or you don't, let us know because we can do both,' she said.
Jeannerett got her start in a whole different form of hair — eyelashes — seven years ago.
'I was just doing it out of my house, but I knew that I was in love with lashes and wanted to go for school for that,' she said.
She got her training with the Paris Lash Academy program and previously has worked at locations such as Turning Heads Salon.
'In the process I fell in love with hair, too,' Jeannerrett said. 'Now I get to do things like hair extensions and just get the best of both worlds.' Karmen Jeannerett holds up a selection of hair extension samples alongside Rare Beauty Co. business partner Avery Atkin. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
Atkin said she wound up partnering with Jeannerett — her soon-to-be sister-in-law — and fellow Craig native Brittany Nations for their own business in somewhat of a whirlwind process. They will also have several part-time workers on staff who will be coming from Grand Junction.
'We're lucky to have people who can offer things like that so we can help more clientele,' Jeannerett said.
Atkin said the process of setting up shop and building a client base has shown her how capable she can be while still in her teen years.
'I never expected to be here at such a young age, but it's been really cool,' she said.
While she has a few years on her business partner, Jeannarett said she's happy to have someone to share the experience.
'I have just as many questions as she does when it comes to opening a business, so we kind of get to learn together, which is comforting,' she said. Avery Atkin, left, and Karmen Jeannerett show off the boutique element of Rare Beauty Co. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press

title: Lance Scranton: Get ready for school
author: Lance Scranton
description: Like it, love it, resist it or embrace it, it doesn't matter as we get ready to wind up that school clock and begin another year preparing future generations. It is evident that some of...
content:
Like it, love it, resist it or embrace it, it doesn't matter as we get ready to wind up that school clock and begin another year preparing future generations.
It is evident that some of us are getting a little bit older if you watched any of the 2024 Olympics and wondered how 'that' is an Olympic sport. But it is and, as the games move to Los Angeles in 2028, there will be even more things happening that prove one thing: The more we hang onto the past, the less we enjoy the future.
School is much the same as young people return to our buildings and all the changes become evident very quickly. No matter the extent of the preparation, there are always surprises that can either send us into a whirlwind of emotional turmoil or help us understand that every school year is unique. Sometimes you look at an Olympic event and think to yourself, 'How did they decide to approve something like that as an actual competition?'
Sometimes the best way to approach a school year is to realize that the changes reflect the fact that our future depends less and less on us and more and more on those we struggle to understand. As some of us enter our third decade in teaching, it is very evident that young people think differently about our future than we do and all that is required for the human race to move ahead is for us to step aside, offer up some wisdom and take on an explorer's attitude — not sure what's beyond the horizon but I'm gonna do my best to make sure we get there safely.
As you ponder what's ahead for this school year, it's imperative to remember three of the key constants in the life of a school year:
There will be surprises — when things don't go to plan we should always understand that it is more about how we respond than what has actually happened.
You will be disappointed — life has a way of humbling every one of us when we think we have it all figured out and we are sure that success is guaranteed.
We will all get through it — entering my 32nd year in education has taught me that if I care enough to still try and make a difference, I am!
The biggest difference we can make as a community is to realize how important the school year is in the development of our future, manage our expectations, embrace inevitable changes and do our best to get them to the horizon as safely as possible.

title: Fifth Quarter series starts after Moffat County football's home opener
author: Staff Report
description: Northwest Colorado groups will be bringing back a popular feature for Moffat County students. The Fifth Quarter events for Craig's high school and middle school students will start anew beginning…
content:
Northwest Colorado groups will be bringing back a popular feature for Moffat County students.
The Fifth Quarter events for Craig's high school and middle school students will start anew beginning Friday, Aug. 30 following Moffat County football's game against Steamboat Springs.
The event, starting between 9-10:30 p.m. depending on the game length, will be a paint party with neon washable paint sprayed on participants during dancing in the parking lot outside the MCHS weight room.
Hot dogs, chips and raffle prizes will also be available. Black or white clothing is encouraged.
Fifth Quarter is a collaboration of Bear River Young Life, Moffat County Youth Action Council, Partners for Youth and Communities That Care.
For more information, contact mackenzie@partnersyouth.org .

title: Moffat County fall sports back in business
author: Andy Bockelman
description: With a return to the classroom last week, Moffat County fall sports seasons are underway as athletes look to pick up where they left off last year. Back in the swing As is customary, the...
content:
Moffat County's Kolten Vasquez tees off during a 2023 tournament. MCHS boys golf is several events into the season, including tournaments in Cedaredge, Aspen, and Carbondale.
Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
With a return to the classroom last week, Moffat County fall sports seasons are underway as athletes look to pick up where they left off last year.
Back in the swing
As is customary, the boys golf team is the first to get going this fall, with the biggest turnout coach Tim Adams has yet seen.
'A lot of this has been because of our junior golf program, that's helped a lot of these guys decide to come out this year,' Adams said.
With 16 total players, Adams also has coaching assistance from Trini Loya and former Moffat County High School player Lance Brackett.
So far, the more seasoned players have been jockeying to lead in score with each tournament. Senior JW Yapoujian shot an 85 and placed eighth at Cedaredge's Bruin Invitational on Aug. 8.
At the Aug. 12 Aspen Invite, senior Jayden Evenson notched a personal-best 82.
'I was putting great. Aspen isn't very long, so I didn't have to worry about drives as much,' he said.
The Aug. 13 Longhorn Class at River Valley Ranch saw junior Kolten Vasquez — the team's lone returning state qualifier — shoot an 89.
'We've had a different leader each time, so it looks like every Bulldog has his day,' Adams said. 'Those three are all pretty solid.'
Seniors Trayson Carlson and Stone Balleck are in their first year in the program, their first year competing but by no means their first time playing the sport.
'I've always played golf, and then just thought, 'why not try the team senior year?'' Carlson said. 'Practices have been pretty fun so far.'
With school now underway, MCHS golf will have a hiatus until Aug. 26, and the Dogs' home tourney will take place Sept. 9 at Yampa Valley Golf Course. Myka Grajeda turns a corner during barrel racing at Moffat County Fairgrounds. Grajeda won the event Sunday, Aug. 18. Courtesy Photo
Ready and raring to ride
The Moffat County rodeo program's beginning to the fall portion of the schedule began in none other than its home arena Saturday and Sunday at Moffat County Fairgrounds.
MoCo cowboys are tackling new events this season, picking up some sizable point counts in their first rodeo of the schedule.
Cutter Barnes placed fourth in both days of boys cutting, while Jesse Grajeda made an early appearance on the leaderboard in his first year of high school competition, taking sixth each day in the rifle shoot.
After competing at the national event this summer, senior Jolene Rhyne showed she may just be back at that level, placing second in goat tying the first day and fourth the second day. Likewise, junior Myka Grajeda was runner-up in breakaway roping on Saturday, followed by a win in barrel racing on Sunday.
'I feel great about it,' Grajeda said. 'I'm already sitting in third in barrels and fourth in breakaway overall after this weekend. My expectations this year are really just focusing on my horses and letting them do their jobs and I do mine so we can hopefully make it to the top again.'
MCHS rodeo will have a brief fall season with upcoming events in Colorado Springs, Cortez and Grand Junction in the coming weeks before a break until April. Moffat County's Zach Hedman tears down the sideline during a 2023 game. MCHS football starts its season on the road in Denver this weekend. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
Gridiron guts
Bulldog football gets going this weekend with a Friday road game in Denver against the John F. Kennedy Commanders.
A MoCo crew that went further than any in decades — making it to the 2A semifinals for the first time since 1993 — will have some different configurations this fall after graduating many players from last season.
However, the Dogs will retain much of their talent up front: seniors Cody Dade, Adam Delay and Clayton Vandersluis look to keep the reputation they cultivated last year as the top offensive line in 2A ball, as designated by MileHigh Prep Report.
While linemen will be protecting a largely different lineup of backfield athletes, among the strong returners is senior Zach Hedman, the top returning rusher from 2023, who posted nearly 600 ground yards as a junior, scoring seven touchdowns.
Hedman, a CHSAA All-State Honorable Mention last year, is also the top returning tackler for the Dogs, with 75 hits as a linebacker, while Vandersluis is the returning leader in sacks with four.
Following this week's away game, MCHS will have back-to-back home events the next two weeks, hosting Steamboat Springs Aug. 30 and Berthoud Sept. 6. Moffat County's Mena Tucker stretches for a hit in 2023. Bulldog volleyball starts the season with a Rangely tournament this weekend. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
At home and away
The schedule will be underway for all Bulldog sports this week, as Bulldog boys soccer kicks off their year with a home opener at 4 p.m. Friday against Eagle Valley.
The same day, MoCo cross country will be off and running at the Fraser Valley Invitational in Granby hosted by Middle Park, while volleyball players will hit the court for a two-day tournament in Rangely.
Meanwhile, the newest Bulldog team will see its first competition as a group as MoCo softball takes on challengers at Saturday's Lyons Round Robin. Moffat County's Karson Fedinec comes down the final stretch during the regional race in 2023. MCHS cross country starts the season in Granby this weekend. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press More Like This, Tap A Topic sports

content:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints will hold a two-day local conference on Sept. 7 and 8.
Meetings will be inside the Craig chapel of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints at 1295 W. Ninth St. and are open to anyone who would like to know more.
Speakers will include church leaders serving in the Vernal Temple, the Denver South mission area and local church officials of the Craig Stake.
The Sept. 7 session for adults will be from 5-7 p.m., and the Sunday session for all ages will be from 10 a.m.-noon on Sept. 9. Visitors are welcome.

title: Craig Press expands coverage with new regional reporting team for Colorado's Western Slope
author: Staff Report
description: Swift Communications, the parent company of the Craig Press, is launching a regional reporting team to cover the most pressing issues on Colorado's Western Slope. The strategic move aims to deliver…
content:
Swift Communications, the parent company of the Craig Press, is launching a regional reporting team to cover the most pressing issues on Colorado's Western Slope.
The strategic move aims to deliver more in-depth analysis and reporting on the intersecting issues facing the mountain communities where Swift operates nine publications and employs more than 40 journalists.
Swift Communications is a subsidiary of West Virginia-based Ogden Newspapers, which publishes over 50 daily newspapers in 18 states stretching from New York to Hawaii.
The team will consist of four reporters based in Colorado and will be led by Andrew Maciejewski, the editor of the Summit Daily News in Summit County.
Maciejewski, a graduate of Indiana University's Media School in Bloomington, came to the Summit Daily News in March 2022 after serving as the executive editor of the Central Indiana News Group, leading a team of 18 reporters and editors across a five-county region. His passion for journalism lies in government accountability, municipal finance and taxpayer-funded project oversight.
'While all of our communities are unique in their own ways, rural resort towns face many of the same issues but approach them in different ways,' Maciejewski said. 'With our reporters living across the mountains, Front Range and Western Slope, my goal for this team is to write stories that allow our communities to collaborate on finding solutions to our challenges.' Andrew Maciejewski
A complex array of issues intersect on Colorado's Western Slope — a region known for ski boots and cowboy boots. The new reporting team's mandate is to cover how those issues impact the daily lives of residents and the millions of visitors who come to Colorado's High Country each year to recreate.
Key areas of focus for the new reporting team will include housing and real estate, outdoors and recreation, wildlife, the environment, water, the ski industry, transportation, health, education, business, public safety, equity and immigration, the state legislature, regional politics, and arts and entertainment. Elliott Wenzler Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
Elliott Wenzler, a native of Nashville, Tennessee, and a graduate of the University of Arkansas in Fayetteville, has been covering Western Slope politics from her home base in Denver since joining Swift in October 2023.
Wenzler has lived in Colorado since 2019 and previously worked for The Colorado Sun and Colorado Community Media. Her beat includes the state Capitol and Colorado's congressional delegation representing the Western Slope as well as politics in the region. Ali Longwell
Ali Longwell grew up in Colorado and began her career in journalism after graduating from the University of Denver in 2016. She has worked and written for several magazines on the Front Range including 5280 Magazine, Colorado Biz Magazine, Denver Life Magazine and spent two years covering enterprise technology for SDxCentral.
Longwell joined the Vail Daily in March 2021 where she was the lead reporter covering the town of Vail and covered education in Eagle County and the health care industry. Her reporting for the regional team will focus on the environment and water, wildlife, health, and arts and entertainment. Andrea Terés-Martínez
Andrea Terés-Martínez joined the Glenwood Springs Post Independent as its assistant editor in September 2023. Born in Guadalajara, Mexico, and raised in Boise, Idaho, she attended Boise State University, where she was editor-in-chief of the university newspaper, The Arbiter.
Terés-Martínez also interned as a reporter for the Idaho Statesman and, more recently, was a publishing editor intern for The Wall Street Journal in New York. At the Post Independent, Terés-Martínez has covered business and development, Latino affairs, housing issues, and civic government in Garfield County. Her reporting for the regional team will focus on education, business, public safety and equity and immigration. Robert Tann
Robert Tann has been covering county government, education and housing for the Summit Daily News since December of 2022. Before that, he worked at Colorado Community Media where he covered local government and housing in the Denver Metro area. Tann was born in London, England and raised in Aurora, Colorado.
He attended the University of Colorado at Boulder where he served as editor-in-chief of the online student news website. He has interned and freelanced for several Colorado media outlets including The Colorado Sun, Colorado Politics and the Daily Camera in Boulder. His reporting for the regional team will focus on housing and real estate, transportation, the outdoors, and Colorado's recreation and ski industries.

title: Moffat County volleyball sets new tone at Rangely tourney
author: Andy Bockelman
description: Though they've seen some new challenges early in the schedule, adversity has been beneficial for Moffat County volleyball players. The Bulldogs went 2-2 during the weekend's Rangely Invitational…
content:
Moffat County's Sofia Vanzo aims a shot against West Grand during the Rangley Invitational Saturday, Aug. 24, 2024.
Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
Though they've seen some new challenges early in the schedule, adversity has been beneficial for Moffat County volleyball players.
The Bulldogs went 2-2 during the weekend's Rangely Invitational Tournament Friday and Saturday, finishing third in their pool and fifth overall among eight teams.
The first match saw Dove Creek claim 25-13 and 25-11 wins, but the MoCo girls found their footing in the next round, falling 25-20 only to bounce back with 25-18 and 15-13 victories for the 2-1 'W' over Plateau Valley.
Saturday saw similar energy as the Dogs faced West Grand and Debeque, losing 2-1 to the Mustangs (23-25, 25-21, 11-15) before sweeping the Dragons in two sets, 27-25 and 25-20.
Senior Caitlyn Adams led the team in kills with 31 across four games, including 13 against West Grand. Sophomore Adrian Profumo had 13 total, nine of which came against Plateau Valley.
Senior Mena Tucker and junior Bella Vanzo each had eight kills in the weekend.
As one of two setters on the floor, Profumo had 25 assists, while senior Moriah Hodnefield notched 38.
The team combined for 13 aces as well as 10 blocks during the tourney, though it was the persistence against every opponent that coach Becca Caldwell most appreciated. The Moffat County varsity volleyball team gathers following the Rangley Invitational Saturday, Aug. 24, 2024. The team went 2-2 with wins over Plateau Valley and Debeque. Top row, from left: manager Keyara Bohrer, Adrian Profumo, Mena Tucker, Bella Vanzo, Sofia Vanzo, Caitlyn Adams, Olivia Cordova. Bottom row: Keona Bolton, Ariana Buchanan, Moriah Hodnefield, coach Becca Caldwell. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
'Their defense is the best I've seen in all my years I've been coaching,' she said. 'They are super scrappy on the floor and hardly let anything drop. Our offense will slowly progress over time, and I think they'll be able to do really well.'
Bulldog volleyball has been facing a different dynamic with practices this fall. Renovations to the MCHS gym floor have led Sage and her athletes to work in the Sandrock Elementary School facilities, with most sessions going later than usual. Moffat County's Caitlyn Adams goes up for a hit against Debeque during the Rangely Invitational Saturday, Aug. 24, 2024. Andy Bockelman/Craig Press
'They're working hard until 8 o'clock every night,' Caldwell said.
Having the rapid-fire introduction to the season with a tournament format in the opening weekend was far more beneficial for the group, she added.
The Bulldogs will travel to Steamboat Springs on Sept. 3, and players look far more ready to face the Sailors than this time last year.
'They have good attitudes this year, they want to work hard and want to be here,' Caldwell said. 'I'm excited about the love they have for each other and for the game. That will help us a lot this year.' Moffat County's Ariana Buchanan receives a serve by Debeque during the Rangely Invitational Saturday, Aug. 24, 2024. title: Craig kids show skills with junior golf finale
author: Andy Bockelman
description: You never know where the next Tiger Woods prodigy may pop up, and the young duffers of Northwest Colorado showed they have bright futures on the links. The Yampa Valley Youth Golf Club hosted its...
content:
The junior golf program players, coaches and parents pose as part of the Drive, Chip & Putt Challenge at Yampa Valley Golf Course Monday, Aug. 19, 2024.
Courtesy Photo
You never know where the next Tiger Woods prodigy may pop up, and the young duffers of Northwest Colorado showed they have bright futures on the links.
The Yampa Valley Youth Golf Club hosted its inaugural Drive, Chip & Putt Challenge on Aug. 19 at Yampa Valley Golf Course, with players from ages 5 to 13 showing their talents.
After 10 weeks of practice, young athletes demonstrated their capabilities in driving, chipping and putting.
Rather than the rules of stroke play, golfers were trying to get a higher score based on the distance and straightness of drives, the accuracy of chipping onto the green and the ability to sink a putt — or at least be the one closest to the pin.
Each player got a cumulative score based on their combined efforts in the three sections, with Camden Loya winning the 5-7 age group, Trace Binder the victor for ages 8-9 and Jack Veenstra the winner in the 10-13 group.
While 16 young golfers competed in the event, about twice that many participated in the junior golf sessions over the summer.
Trini Loya coached the group, which also included high school ages.
'We pretty much worked on fundamentals, helping them with their stance and just hitting the ball,' he said. 'Then we got into some of the funner events like chipping into a hula hoop. We geared them more toward being able to do that challenge, learn how to drive far correctly.'
Loya added that while most players were brand-new to the game, their progress showed greatly nearly three months after the start of the clinic.
While some competitors barely could hold up a club at first, helping them figure out the mechanics was worth it.
'By the end of it, I think they all got a pretty good grasp on how to play and etiquette on the course,' Loya said. 'We didn't want to get too strict about anything, just have fun with all of it.' More Like This, Tap A Topic sports

title: Man killed in off-road vehicle accident identified
description: The Routt County Coroner's office has identified the man who died in an off-road highway vehicle accident Wednesday as 88-year-old James G. Floyd. Coroner Mitch Locke said details about the cause of…
content:
The Routt County Coroner's office has identified the man who died in an off-road highway vehicle accident Wednesday as 88-year-old James G. Floyd.
Coroner Mitch Locke said details about the cause of the accident, which occurred on a property near Pagoda in West Routt County, are not yet known.
Emergency personnel from multiple agencies responded to the scene Wednesday morning after an individual discovered the vehicle being driven by Floyd, referred to as an OHV, upside down and submerged in a body of water on a property on Routt County Road 29.
According to emergency dispatch communications, the OHV had reportedly been submerged for approximately 1-2 hours before first responders reached the scene and performed life saving techniques including CPR for roughly 40 minutes.
The property where the incident occurred is in a remote section of unincorporated Routt County south of Hayden and southeast of Craig near the Pagoda neighborhood.

title: Man dies after off-road vehicle flips into water in West Routt
author: Staff Report
description: A West Routt County resident died Wednesday afternoon after the off-road highway vehicle he was driving was discovered upside down and submerged in water on a property near Routt County Road 29 in the…
content:
A West Routt County resident died Wednesday afternoon after the off-road highway vehicle he was driving was discovered upside down and submerged in water on a property near Routt County Road 29 in the Pagoda area.
According to emergency dispatch communications, the vehicle referred to as an OHV had reportedly been submerged for approximately 1-2 hours before first responders reached the scene.
The man, who authorities believed to be in his 80s, was pronounced deceased at 12:24 p.m. Wednesday after emergency personnel performed an extrication, as well as CPR and life-saving procedures for roughly 40 minutes, according to the emergency radio traffic.
Multiple agencies responded to the incident with Hayden police and West Routt Fire arriving first at the scene.
First responders from Moffat County including Craig Fire and the Routt County Sheriff's Office also responded along with a Classic Air Medical crew that arrived by helicopter and assisted with the resuscitation attempts.
The property where the incident occurred is in a remote section of unincorporated Routt County south of Hayden and southeast of Craig near the Pagoda neighborhood.

title: Obituary: Cameron Martin
description: June 24, 1997 – August 26, 2024 Cameron Martin died Monday, August 26, 2024, at his home after losing his battle of many years with depression. He was 27. Funeral services were held at 10...
content:
Obituaries Obituaries | Sep 4, 2024 Cameron Martin
Provided Photo
June 24, 1997 – August 26, 2024
Cameron Martin died Monday, August 26, 2024, at his home after losing his battle of many years with depression. He was 27. Funeral services were held at 10 a.m., Friday, August 30, 2024, at St. Michael's Catholic Church. Interment followed at Craig Cemetery. Cameron was born June 24, 1997, in Aurora, CO to Diane (Earle) and Cedric Martin. He moved to Craig with his mother and older brother, Casey in 1998. Diane married Rich King on April 17, 1999, and they settled at the family ranch just south of Craig where Cameron grew up. He spent his childhood years with his wonderful brothers and sister, developing a love for learning and a passion for music very early on in his life. Cameron participated in band and excelled academically throughout his school years, graduating with honors from Moffat County High School in 2015. He then continued his musical studies at the University of Colorado at Colorado Springs, again graduating in the top five percent of his class in 2019 with a Bachelor of Arts in Music Composition and Sound Design. Cameron's entire family enjoyed watching his talent develop throughout his life, from playing the clarinet in elementary school, to composing his own music as an adult. Cameron's desire to learn continued after he achieved his BA degree, and he was working on a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science at the University of Colorado Boulder at the time of his passing. He also spent many hours assisting with technical sound support and systems at St. Michael's Catholic Church in Craig. He is survived by his parents, Virgil Richard and Diane King of Craig and Cedric Martin of Arizona; his grandparents, Leon and Rose (Vallejos) Earle of Craig; his 105- year-old great-grandmother, Florela Vallejos of Bosque, NM; his older brother and sister-in-law Casey (Kaci) Meek-Martin, and their children, Nikolai and Aubrielle, of Castle Rock; his younger brother Carlin King of Craig; and his younger sister Cayden King of Craig. He is preceded in death by his grandparents, Dick and Jane King of Craig.
Cameron was a grandson, son, brother, uncle, nephew, cousin, and dear friend. His entire family will dearly miss his kindness, his music, his enthusiasm for fireworks and amusement park rides, and challenging his siblings in all games, whether electronic or board games. We'll miss his smile and laughter that radiated love most of all.

title: Not opposed to housing miners, residents take issue with proposed location of temporary man camp in Moffat County
author: Eli Pace
description: A proposal to construct a man camp in Moffat County is being framed as an economic benefit for the community, ensuring that dozens of mine workers will spend their hard-earned dollars at local…
content:
On Tuesday, Sept. 10, 2024, Moffat County Commissioners are scheduled to revisit a request to allow the construction of temporary housing units for TwentyMile Mine workers at 3037 E. Victory Way in Moffat County.
Peabody Energy/Courtesy
A proposal to construct a man camp in Moffat County is being framed as an economic benefit for the community, ensuring that dozens of mine workers will spend their hard-earned dollars at local businesses and stores, but a number of residents who live near the proposed site remain wary.
The request for a temporary-use permit comes from from Mesa B&B LLC, which is owned by Bud Bower, the owner of Bower Brothers Construction. Bower is requesting to erect four temporary five-bedroom units and accompanying accessory buildings to house up to 20 mine workers at 3037 E. Victory Way through 2028.
According to the applicant, the housing units would be used to lodge only workers from the TwentyMile Mine between Hayden and Oak Creek owned by Peabody Energy.
The newspaper previously misreported that there are already temporary housing units on the property. However, no units currently exist there.
Instead, the applicant has expressed a desire to move an existing man camp in Routt County to the proposed site in Moffat County, which would increase the number of requested temporary housing units from four to 20. The request for the additional units to would come through the permit's renewal process. The man camp in Routt County includes 16 units and houses up to 48 workers.
Addressing Moffat County Commissioners on Aug. 13, Planning Department staff said the temporary housing units could be set up or taken down in a weekend with all of their services — water, septic and electric — remaining above ground.
County staff said they reached out to officials in Routt County and were told there have been no issues with the existing man camp. The camp's permit sunsets in November 2025 and the owners have expressed a desire to relocate to Moffat County in spring 2026.
County staff noted two of Moffat County's Planning and Zoning commissioners voted not to recommend approving the application based on the road and placement of the project, but would possibly reconsider if another location were proposed. A third member of the planning and zoning commission voted to recommend approval with conditions.
Speaking at the Aug. 13 hearing before county commissioners, Bower talked about the difficulty workers have finding housing and said the facility would be strictly for mine employees and not anyone else including their own families.
He said the workers who stay at the man camp in Routt County are not allowed overnight guests and the facility has mechanisms and policies in place to ensure a safe environment for the men and women who live there and work for the mine.
'It has been basically hassle-free for the employees and for the people that clean the facility, that service the facility and the mine,' Bower said. 'It is a definite — I think that, I don't know the exact numbers … but I think the bookings that we have had are well over 4,000 currently to date in less than 18 months.'
He continued by highlighting the potential economic benefits that could come as a result of the workers staying in Craig, likening them to people from out of town who visit as tourists.
'If you take an average of 60 people that use the facility at any given point in time, at its full capacity, if we're in Moffat County, you are talking about 60 people spending an average of $150 per day into the community of Craig,' Bower said.
The proposed capacity numbers represent a concern to some of the neighbors and nearby residents who worry about the effect the man camp might have on them and their surroundings.
One neighbor asked county commissioners about the code that allows temporary housing, saying the code mandates that temporary employee housing can only be used for workers at a 'temporary worksite.' The resident said she doesn't see how the mine could qualify as a temporary worksite.
She also said the man camp would not be compatible with other land uses in the area and expressed concern about increased traffic from it, adding that she and her neighbors have been a part of the community for a long time and the effects on them should also be considered.
Citing the size of the proposed project, another neighbor brought up the additional trips for things like garbage collection, housekeeping and more, as well as environmental concerns and snow removal.
'In my mind, moving the existing man camp from Hayden to Craig mostly benefits the man camp operators, but it adds 50 miles roundtrip every day to the workers who use it, so who really benefits?' Curtis Elwood asked. 'It doesn't add much to the tax rolls of the county. My guess is that most of the man camp occupants shop in Craig already, and it adds no benefit to East Victory Way, to our residential-agricultural community, and may even harm the value of what we have worked so hard to maintain.'
He ended by saying there are better locations for a proposal like this in the county. Other neighbors also spoke out against the project, saying it would lead to more traffic on an already dangerous road and diminish the value of their own properties.
Many of the complaints focused on the proposed location, and speakers qualified their statements by saying they were not in opposition to housing mine workers in Moffat County. A couple of people also spoke up in favor of the man camp.
Citing unanswered questions, Moffat County Commissioners took no action on the permit application. The matter was continued until their next meeting Sept. 10.

title: Health Column: Memorial Regional Health's Pain Management Team offers iovera — Treatment involving cold therapy to block nerve pain
author: Memorial Regional Health
description: Memorial Regional Health CRNAs and pain management specialists Alfred Maina and Trey Gorham recently traveled to Houston for training in the use of a new treatment called iovera. 'We are committed to…
content:
Memorial Regional Health's Pain Management Team offers Iovera, an innovative cold therapy treatment that targets nerve pain, helping patients find relief. The therapy uses precise, controlled freezing to block pain signals in targeted areas, such as the knee, without affecting surrounding tissues.
Memorial Regional Health/Courtesy photo
Memorial Regional Health CRNAs and pain management specialists Alfred Maina and Trey Gorham recently traveled to Houston for training in the use of a new treatment called iovera.
'We are committed to providing the most up-to-date and evidence-based treatments for managing chronic and acute pain in our communities,' Maina said. 'Iovera is a proprietary treatment involving cold therapy to block nerve pain. It's great for chronic knee pain, post-operative pain after knee replacement, nerve pain in the lower extremities and pain management after rib fractures.'
First Maina and Gorham identify the target nerves with ultrasound. Then they inject numbing medication into area to make the procedure more comfortable. Finally, they place the small needle at the tip of the handheld iovera device into the target nerve. This freezes the nerve, stopping the transmission of the pain signal.
'We repeat this process for the three or four main nerves that supply sensation to the area that is hurting,' Maina said. 'The result is that patients can have a few months of relief, and the treatment can be repeated as needed in the months to come.'
Many people with chronic joint pain are used to getting cortisone shots to subdue their discomfort. But iovera can be a better option because cortisone is a steroid, and steroids can raise blood glucose levels, which is a problem for people with diabetes or prediabetes.
'Also, iovera is a better option for people with severe joint degeneration,' Maina said. 'For those patients, cortisone injections are mostly ineffective.'
Iovera can also be used a few weeks prior to knee surgery. This reduces pain for the patient pre-surgery and lasts through and after the surgery, reducing post-surgical pain as well.
Finally, because iovera is a freezing technique, it doesn't involve medication. 'Limiting the impact of opioids in our community and helping improve quality of life continue to be the main driver of our pain management program,' Maina said.
To find out if iovera might be right for you, make an appointment with Maina or Gorham by calling 970-826-2400.
'We'll do a comprehensive evaluation to determine if you are a candidate for iovera or any of the other treatment approaches we use in managing pain,' Maina said. 'And if you're going to have knee surgery, ask your surgeon about the possibility of receiving iovera two to three weeks before the surgery. They can place a referral to our pain management team.'
Iovera is covered by most insurances.
'We have a team of people who will ensure that the appropriate prior authorizations are performed prior to scheduling the patient for the procedure,' Maina said.
